title: Clint Black says Billy Joel's 'Uncle Daddy' warning changed his life
summary: Clint Black reveals how a Billy Joel interview about being an "Uncle Daddy" reshaped his approach to fatherhood after welcoming daughter Lily.
story: Clint Black says Billy Joel's warning about becoming an "Uncle Daddy" inspired him to spend his daughter's early years at home instead of on the road. The country music star has a new memoir, "Killin' Time."
When Clint Black and Lisa Hartman Black welcomed their only child, Lily, in 2001, the country star made fatherhood his top priority to avoid becoming an "Uncle Daddy."

Black opens up about that decision in his new memoir, "Killin' Time," named after his triple-platinum 1989 debut album. The Grammy winner reflects on his upbringing, his meteoric rise to fame and a career that has included more than 20 million records sold.
The 64-year-old singer told Fox News Digital he came across an interview with Billy Joel, and the "Piano Man" singer's words stayed with him.
CLINT BLACK AND LISA HARTMAN BLACK'S ONE RULE THAT HAS KEPT THEIR MARRIAGE STRONG FOR NEARLY 35 YEARS
From left: Lily Pearl Black, Clint Black and Lisa Hartman Black attend the BMI Country Awards at BMI on Nov. 18, 2025, in Nashville, Tennessee. (Erika Goldring/Getty Images for BMI)

"I saw an interview with Billy Joel, and he was talking about being gone too much. He said he'd come home... and he called it being 'Uncle Daddy,'" said Black. "That was long before we knew we wanted a child, but I remember it sticking with me."
"Killin’ Time: My Life and Music" by Clint Black is available now. (Harper Influence)

In "Killin' Time," Black recalled Joel saying life on the road often left him feeling more like an "Uncle Daddy" than a father. The comment stayed with Black for years and ultimately reshaped how he balanced his career and family.
American songwriter and singer Billy Joel records his album "The Bridge" at The Power Station recording studio on Aug. 20, 1986, in New York, N.Y. (Getty Images)
"I didn't cut out activities completely when Lily was born," said Black.
WATCH: CLINT BLACK EXPLAINS WHY HE REFUSED TO BE AN ‘UNCLE DADDY’

"I did about 15 shows a year just to take care of the band and crew members.... I read a book or two, and I can't remember which one, but the author was talking about secure attachment for a child — who the child feels is their secure attachment, the person they look to in moments of fright. And if you want to be a secure attachment for your child, it's something you earn in the first three years of their life."
Clint Black and Lily Pearl Black attend the BMI Country Awards at BMI in Nashville on Nov. 18, 2025. (Getty Images for BMI)

"So that was the number," he continued. "Three years of mostly being home, only going out and doing these small bits of work. I did some work at home, working on music... but I was around to be a dad. It wasn't great for my career, but I wouldn't change a thing. I wouldn't trade a better career for that attachment or the closeness I have with my daughter."
For Black, fatherhood came after years of heartbreak. In the book, he revealed that he and the former "Knots Landing" actress suffered four pregnancy losses before welcoming Lily.

Clint Black holds his daughter Lily with his wife Lisa Hartman Black backstage after the KIPP Rhythm & String Orchestra performance at Carnegie Hall benefiting the KIPP Academy New York on Dec. 4, 2002. (Richard Corkery/NY Daily News Archive via Getty Images)

"Trying to have a baby was not something that we had set out to do," he said. "And then, at one point, we realized we had better talk about this and find out where we both stood. And once we decided we wanted to have a child, we really, really wanted to have a child. So when we ran into problems with the miscarriages, it started to hurt. But we kept our hopes up."

"'Little Pearl' started playing at the instant our daughter came out into the world," wrote Clint Black. "After all of the bedrest and the accompanying worries, Lily Pearl Black arrived on her due date, right as her song began playing. Showbiz kid?" (Variety via Getty Images)
"It was still scary getting through it," he admitted. "It wasn't smooth sailing, but it was sailing. We have a 25-year-old daughter now, and she is just a joy."
Black said that when Lily was born, he embraced fatherhood without hesitation.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Clint Black and Lisa Hartman Black welcomed Lily on May 8, 2001. (WireImage)

"I think the biggest lesson I've learned from fatherhood is — I'm tempted to say patience — but I don't think that's it," he explained. "I think it's that I can do a lot more than I thought I could. I could have a career, travel, do all of that, come home, be active as a dad, go to basketball practice, volleyball games and school events."
Clint Black is seen here with his daughter Lily, his wife Lisa Hartman Black and Cinderella. (WireImage/Getty Images)

"Taking her to bouncy playhouses, [watching] 'The Wiggles,' 'Bear in the Big Blue House' and 'Wicked,'" he said with a smile. "All the plays and all that stuff. I wouldn't have thought that I could do it all. But I have, and I've surpassed my own expectations. And that's through devoting myself to her, my wife and being present."
These days, Black is back on the road, and every so often, fans can catch Lily sharing the stage with him.

Lily Pearl Black, Clint Black and Lisa Hartman Black perform during the "America Salutes You 2023 Concert For Gratitude" at The Fisher Center for the Performing Arts in Nashville, on Dec. 15, 2023. (Terry Wyatt/Getty Images)
"I'm still doing 80 to 90 cities a year on tour, taking Lily and Lisa with me at times," he said. "They have toured with me. Those are the best tours."
"It's surprising," he reflected. "I went into fatherhood ready to do whatever it took. But the fear I had was, 'Is this going to be too much? I won't be able to do it all.' But I did."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Lily Pearl Black, Clint Black and Lisa Hartman Black attend the world premiere of Lifetime's "When I Said I Do" at Franklin Theatre in Franklin, Tennessee, on May 12, 2026. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)
Even today, Black said he's still in awe when he watches his daughter perform alongside him.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Lily Pearl Black, Clint Black and Lisa Hartman Black attend the "America Salutes You" 2023 concert at The Fisher Center for the Performing Arts in Nashville, on Dec. 15, 2023. (Tibrina Hobson/Getty Images)

"Watching Lily perform right next to me on stage took me a while to adjust to," he admitted. "For a while, I was just the adoring father. I had to learn to be a guy in the band playing to an audience and enjoy what she’s doing and seeing her perform so well without having that be my focus on stage. I think it becomes distracting to the audience if they’re watching us, and they’re watching me with a shifted focus."
"But seeing her beside me, it's a gift," he added.
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: 'Blue Lagoon' star Christopher Atkins says alcohol cost him iconic 'Footloose' role before getting sober
summary: The "Blue Lagoon" star revealed at Fanboy Expo Knoxville how partying cost him the "Footloose" lead and reflected on nearly 40 years of sobriety.
story: The actor, who was a sex symbol in the '80s, recalled playing the love interest of Brooke Shields and Linda Gray. Atkins now wants to work behind-the-scenes as a filmmaker.
Christopher Atkins claims his drinking cost him the lead role in "Footloose," which ultimately went to Kevin Bacon.
The "Blue Lagoon" actor looked back at his career during a recent appearance at Fanboy Expo Knoxville in Tennessee, which celebrates pop culture and nostalgia, People magazine reported.
According to the outlet, the 65-year-old actor said filmmakers behind the 1984 classic wanted to meet with him before making their final casting decision, but he wasn't able to pull it off.
BRAT PACK ICON ANDREW MCCARTHY SAYS DRINKING 'DERAILED MY CAREER ENTIRELY'

Christopher Atkins, left, who starred opposite Brooke Shields, center, in 1980's "The Blue Lagoon," recently told a panel at the Fanboy Expo Knoxville that he lost the lead role in 1984's "Footloose" to Kevin Bacon, right, because his drinking cost him an important meeting with the filmmakers. (Sonia Moskowitz/Getty Images; CBS via Getty Images)
"I was a mess back then," he told the panel, as quoted by People. "I was partying it up way too much, and they called me in."

"I said... 'I can't go in right now. I've been drinking and carrying on,'" Atkins recalled. "And they said, 'No, they need to see you.' And I went in, and I just blew that audition... I mean, it wasn't even an audition — I had the part, but I was so messed up that they said, 'Yeah, we're going to have to pass on this guy.'"
Atkins was offered the role of Ren in "Footloose," after making his on-screen debut alongside Brooke Shields in "The Blue Lagoon." (Columbia Pictures/Getty Images)
"And I'm almost 40 years sober, so there you go," Atkins added.
WATCH: CHRISTOPHER ATKINS LOOKS BACK AT ‘THE BLUE LAGOON’ AND ‘DALLAS’
The actor also reflected on his breakout role in "The Blue Lagoon" during the discussion. The former teen heartthrob was just 18 when he was cast in the 1980 movie opposite Brooke Shields.
"I'd never done anything before," Atkins explained. "Never wanted to be an actor — I only wanted to play baseball. That was my dream."
Kevin Bacon as Ren in a scene from the movie "Footloose." (CBS/Getty Images)
"I didn't know what a camera looked like. I had no idea what a mark was, and I knew nothing. And I had to jump on an airplane and fly all the way to Fiji," he said.
Actor Christopher Atkins attends CollectorFest New Jersey at Wayne P.A.L. in Wayne, N.J., on Oct. 18, 2020. (Bobby Bank/Getty Images)

"I ended up modeling for [the] Ford Modeling Agency in New York City and auditioned for 'The Blue Lagoon'... And I kept getting called back and called back and called back. And then [after] a couple of months, I didn't hear from them... And then all of a sudden, I got another callback."
The "Dallas" alum said his "whole life changed" after the movie's release.
Christopher Atkins went on to star in "Dallas" opposite Linda Gray. (CBS Photo Archive/Getty Images)

"We were young, and so you're constantly getting this notoriety," Atkins explained. "And the magazines need you to sell their magazines, and you're hot at that time. And so it does get overwhelming... There are times when you're doing interviews, and you have a line of people, and you have to say the same thing to each person because they have the same question."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Brooke Shields and "Blue Lagoon" co-star Christopher Atkins circa 1980 in New York City. (Sonia Moskowitz/Images/Getty Images)
"But it changes your life, because all of a sudden you’re nothing and then you’re on every single grocery store magazine."
Back in 2025, Atkins told Fox News Digital he "didn't know that much" about Shields, then 14, before she joined him on the set of "The Blue Lagoon."
Despite the controversy, "The Blue Lagoon" became a major box office success and made Christopher Atkins an overnight star. (Columbia Pictures/Getty Images)

"I lived on [a] boat off the island [where we were filming]... she hadn't come yet," he said at the time. "She had another week or so before she was going to get here. The director had put her picture up over my bed so that I could start falling in love with her before the movie started. That was my introduction to Brooke Shields."
Actors Christopher Atkins and Brooke Shields in the 1980 movie, "The Blue Lagoon," directed by Randal Kleiser. (Columbia Pictures/Getty Images)

The movie was controversial for depicting the two young characters in a sexual relationship. Shields and the movie's crew have long maintained that she used body doubles for nude scenes and that her hair was glued to her body to avoid exposing her chest, People magazine reported.

"The crew was all Australian," Atkins said. "Back in the day, all the Australian beaches... were topless. It was very natural and freeing for the Australians... And being on a deserted island, there were no tourists, nothing. It was just us on this island... [And] these two kids, in a natural [and deserted] environment, they wouldn't wear clothes. It wouldn't be something that was in the forefront of their minds, that they needed to cover up."
Christopher Atkins and Brooke Shields attend an event celebrating their movie at the Cinerama Dome theater in Hollywood on June 19, 1980. (Robert Ware/WWD/Penske Media via Getty Images)

"As time went on, it just became more and more natural not to have clothes on," Atkins said. "The crew made it very, very easy. Randall [Kleiser], the director, made it very, very easy about it. [The scenes] were absolutely important for the film, but it wasn't grandiose. It wasn't something that was there for the exhibition of the film. He really wanted this to be as natural and as real as possible. I understood that and got that."
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"The Blue Lagoon" sparked controversy for its depiction of teenage sexuality and nudity, despite the filmmakers' use of body doubles and other techniques for certain scenes. (Columbia Pictures/Getty Images)
"By the time I was done leaving that island four and a half months later, it [was] really hard for me to keep my clothes on at a beach," he joked.

People magazine noted that critics largely panned the movie. However, it was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Cinematography. The outlet reported that the movie grossed more than $58 million worldwide, making it the ninth-highest-grossing film of 1980.
Christopher Atkins recently told a panel at the Fanboy Expo Knoxville that he's nearly 40 years sober. (Sonia Moskowitz/Images/Getty Images)
Looking back at his Hollywood career, Atkins said he has no regrets.
Christopher Atkins attends a private screening of the virtual reality short film "Defrost" on Aug. 17, 2015, in Los Angeles. (Paul Redmond/Getty Images)

"I got to a point in my life where I married young," he said. "I wanted to be a dad more than chase the business... When I was 16, I used to teach sailing in Rye, New York, to little kids. From that measly paycheck that I was getting, I used to put a dollar away for someday when I had kids. That's how badly I wanted kids. When I had my two kids, I just did whatever came my way to put food on the table for them and keep working."

In this undated photo, Brooke Shields and Christopher Atkins attend a celebrity Halloween event at the home of Susie Field for the children of Los Angeles Children's Hospital in Beverly Hills. (SGranitz/WireImage)

"I've been blessed," he said. "I've done more than 100 movies and television shows at this point. Now my kids have their kids, and that's pretty remarkable... I've done everything in this business except make my own film. That's the last box I now want to check off... That's what I'm chasing right now, putting some really good projects together... So there are no regrets."

title: 'The Odyssey' star Matt Damon reveals brutal six-month transformation behind Christopher Nolan film
summary: Matt Damon dropped to 167 pounds on a gluten-free diet and grew a real beard for a year to play Odysseus in Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey."
story: The trailer for the Universal Pictures epic 'The Odyssey' starring Matt Damon, Anne Hathaway, Tom Holland, Zendaya, Robert Pattinson and Charlize Theron. Directed by Christopher Nolan.
Matt Damon is opening up about how achieving his dramatic physical transformation for Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey" "just kind of took over my life."

The 55-year-old actor appeared nearly unrecognizable starring as legendary Greek hero Odysseus in the mythological epic, which dominated the global box office after its July 17 release with a roughly $264 million opening weekend — the biggest debut of Nolan's career.
During a recent appearance on "Live with Kelly and Mark," Damon revealed what it took to fulfill the 55-year-old director's vision for the role.
‘THE ODYSSEY’ STAR MATT DAMON REVEALS STRICT DIET CHOICE THAT 'CHANGED MY LIFE' AFTER HIDDEN HEALTH ISSUES

"He said, 'I just want him to look lean and strong like somebody who's a veteran of the Trojan War and can handle himself, but wouldn't pass up a meal if it was offered to him,'" Damon recalled Nolan telling him.
Matt Damon detailed his intense six-month transformation for "The Odyssey." ( Kristy Sparow/Getty Images for Universal Pictures; Melinda Sue Gordon © Universal Studios. All Rights Reserved.)
"And that's kind of the hardest shape to get into, you know, that kind of lean-strong thing," the actor added. "But it just kind of took over my life."

In the movie, which is an adaptation of Homer’s epic poem "The Odyssey," Odysseus spends 10 years trying to return home after fighting in the 10-year Trojan War, enduring shipwrecks, battles with monsters, starvation, imprisonment and constant physical hardship on his journey.
MATT DAMON REFUSES TO PUT BODY IN 'DANGEROUS' SITUATIONS FOR HOLLYWOOD ROLES AFTER TURNING 50
Damon told hosts Kelly Ripa and Mark Consuelos that he underwent an intense six-month process to realistically portray the weathered, battle-hardened warrior.

The "Good Will Hunting" star referenced his January appearance on Travis and Jason Kelce's podcast "New Heights," in which he revealed that he had slimmed down to his "high school" weight for the role. While speaking with the NFL stars, Damon shared, "I used to walk around between 185 and 200 pounds. And I did that whole movie at 167 pounds."

"I was talking to the Kelce brothers on their podcast like six months ago, and we were talking about it," he told Ripa and Consuelos. "It felt more like an athlete's regimen, kind of like those guys who have to just dedicate every moment of their day to thinking about everything."
The actor adopted a strict gluten-free diet to play the Greek hero Odysseus. (Aalok Soni/Getty Images for Universal Pictures)
MARVEL STAR VINCENT D’ONOFRIO SAYS HE ‘CAN’T DO’ KINGPIN TRANSFORMATION ANYMORE
Damon described how he followed a routine in which food portions were measured and every aspect of his diet was carefully monitored.
"Everything's weighed," he said. "It's just very, very intentional about everything."
Damon also reflected on adopting a gluten-free diet to shed the pounds. He noted that he had not previously realized how many food and drink items contain gluten.
"It's in a lot of things, but there are a lot of great things that it's not in," he said, before citing rice and potatoes.
However, Damon acknowledged that he had to make some difficult sacrifices to stay gluten-free.
"Listen, I had to give up beer. That was tough," he said.
"Is there gluten in beer?" Ripa asked.
"There sure is," Damon replied. "Yeah. There are some gluten-free beers though. I'm learning about all this."
"It's in bread. It's in pasta. It's in a lot of the stuff that we love," he added.

Jimmy Gonzales as Cepheus, Matt Damon as Odysseus and Himesh Patel as Eurylochus in "The Odyssey," written, produced, and directed by Nolan. (Melinda Sue Gordon © Universal Studios. All Rights Reserved.)

During a July interview with People magazine, Damon recalled that his commitment to remain gluten-free was tested when his wife Luciana, 50, and his four daughters Alexia, 27, Isabella, 20, Gia, 17, and Stella, 15, visited him while he was filming "The Odyssey" in Italy.
"I promised them I was gonna have pasta with them, and right after I ordered it, I just called the waiter back, and I was like, ‘I’ll just please have a steak instead,’" Damon remembered.
"And the kids were like, ‘but you promised!’ and I said, ‘I’ll have a bite of each of your pastas,’" he continued. "So I took a bite of each of theirs."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
"I was just in it, I just, it was gonna be four or five more months. It’s all or nothing at this point," Damon added.
While speaking with Ripa and Consuelos, Damon explained why he has continued to maintain a gluten-free diet after completing production on "The Odyssey."
"I just felt so much better," he said.
Damon said he has continued to maintain his gluten-free regimen since production on "The Odyssey" wrapped. (Jeff Spicer/Getty Images for Universal Pictures)

Damon has previously opened up about drastically transforming his body for roles. For the 1996 war drama "Courage Under Fire," Damon lost between 40 and 50 pounds in about 100 days to play a Persian Gulf veteran dying from addiction and trauma.
The actor later said his extreme weight loss was dangerous and revealed that a doctor told him that he "could have shrunk my heart permanently."
"I went too far," Damon said via the U.K. outlet Express. "I got sick, and I wouldn’t do that again because it was just too much."

"At the same time, it helped the performance," he continued. "I didn’t have to act at all; I was a wreck. I was getting dizzy spells and hot flashes. I didn’t say anything to anyone for a while because I was afraid I might be really ill."
Meanwhile, Damon has previously said he had a more enjoyable experience when he gained about 30 pounds to play real-life whistleblower Mark Whitacre in 2009's "The Informant!"
"It was very, very easy to gain the weight. Very, very fun," Damon told reporters in 2009, via NBC. "I just basically ate everything I could see for a few months."
However, Damon recently shared that he is no longer willing to subject himself to extreme weight fluctuations for roles.
Damon as Odysseus and Zendaya as Athena in Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey." (Melinda Sue Gordon © Universal Studios. All Rights Reserved.)
While discussing transforming his body for "The Odyssey" in an interview with People magazine, Damon noted, "I didn’t change it in an unhealthy way."
"I think if I had done the opposite and put weight on, that would have been dangerous and it’s not something I’ll do anymore," he continued. "I was happy to do it earlier in my life."
Damon has previously shed light on other aesthetic changes that he made to play Odysseus, including growing a long beard and keeping it for a year.
While speaking with USA Today, Damon said he and Nolan agreed that a fake, hand-laid beard was out of the question due to the water stunts that the actor had to perform for the movie.

"Any movie problem, the best solve is a practical one," Damon said. "In that case, it was like I was going to be thrown around. I was gonna be thrown into the water. Like a beard that wasn't — that didn't stay, you know, a hand-laid beard would just come off in salt water."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

He continued, "And so there was no point trying to hand lay a beard, which I've done for other movies and works very well. But in this case, [Nolan] was like, ‘The only practical solution is just to have the beard.’"
"So I had a big bushy beard for, you know, a year or so. My kids thought I looked like Santa Claus," he added with a laugh.
Damon said he is no longer willing to unhealthily transform his body for a role. (Melinda Sue Gordon © Universal Studios. All Rights Reserved.)

Nolan is known for his commitment to authenticity, which is a hallmark of the Oscar-winning director's filmmaking. "The Odyssey" marked a reunion for Damon and Nolan after they previously collaborated on the hit movies "Interstellar" and "Oppenheimer."
While speaking with Ripa and Consuelos, Damon praised Nolan's directorial style and preference for practical effects.
"It's amazing working with him," Damon said. "He's a great actor's director. He's just so fun to work with."

"And he gets this elite crew," he continued. "They're so good and up for how he wants to do things. He wants to shoot everything in camera. There's no CGI. So if you see a thousand people in a battle, there were a thousand people there. If there are ships in the background of a shot, those are real ships."

"And the amount of coordination it takes between all these departments, that's actually, in this day and age, extraordinary," Damon added. "It really is. It's great to be a part of. It felt like we were doing a movie from 70 years ago, which is very cool."
Damon recalled that he instantly signed on after Nolan asked him to play the centrol role in the film. (Aalok Soni/Getty Images for Universal Pictures)

Damon told Ripa and Consuelos that for him, committing to "The Odyssey" required little deliberation. Recalling the moment Nolan first offered him the lead role, the actor said the director spent about 15 minutes catching up before mentioning he was thinking about going back to work.
"And I'd like to offer you the central role," Damon recalled Nolan saying.
Damon said he immediately accepted, prompting Nolan to ask, "Don't you want to hear what it is?"

"I was like, ‘Sure,'" Damon said. "And he goes, 'It's a two-word pitch: The Odyssey.'"
"My heart skipped a beat," he recalled. "It's an incredible part to play for an actor. The role of a lifetime."

title: Ted Danson wanted to 'stop being a liar' at the end of 'Cheers' saying he 'f---ed up' his life so badly
summary: Ted Danson revealed on his podcast that he "f---ed up" his personal life so badly he didn't even realize that "Cheers" had ended back in 1993.
story: ‘Cheers’ actor Ted Danson tells Fox News Digital why he doesn’t think a reunion will happen in the future.
Ted Danson is getting real about the state of his personal life toward the end of his run on "Cheers."
During a recent episode of his podcast, "Where Everybody Knows Your Name," the 78-year-old actor gave listeners an idea about what his life was like when "Cheers" came to an end in 1993.
"People say, 'What was it like? What did you do when she was over?' I said, 'I had f---ed up my life so much that I didn't even realize 'Cheers' was over,'" he said.
Elsewhere in the conversation, Danson admitted he "barely knew myself" and took a "postgrad grow-up class fast" the last year he was on the hit show.
Danson admits he had messed up his life during the last year of "Cheers." (Robin L Marshall/Getty Images)
TED DANSON WAS SHOCKED WOMEN VIEWED HIM AS A SEX SYMBOL DURING EARLY ‘CHEERS’ DAYS
He described driving to Long Beach to see his mentor, whom he called "amazing," saying he gave him "a whole different kind of therapy spirituality kind of thing."
"I wanted to stop being a liar," he said. "I wanted to be emotionally mature. I wanted to change."
The "Curb Your Enthusiasm" star previously spoke about the end of the series in an August 2025 episode of his podcast, reflecting on the state of his personal life at the time.

When asked by his guest, Charlie Day, if he was afraid of being typecast when the show ended, Danson said "the transition was easy because I blew my personal life up so badly," and he didn't realize the show had ended for a few months "because I was just dealing with myself and my personal stuff."
Danson previously discussed the state of his personal life while filming the back half of "Cheers." (NBCU Photo Bank)

Danson starred on the beloved sitcom as Sam Malone from 1982 to 1993, becoming one of the few cast members to appear in all 273 episodes of the show.
"Cheers" came to an end after 11 seasons, when Danson expressed his desire to pursue other acting opportunities, with executives deciding the show should not go on without him.

"I was changing for the better and working really hard at that, so I thought, 'Might as well jump completely off the cliff,'" he said. "And [there was] a little bit of ... 'If I don't leave now, I may not know if I could do anything else, and I want to see if I can do any other stuff.'"
After his time on "Cheers," Danson starred in "Becker," "Curb Your Enthusiasm" and "CSI: Crime Scene Investigation," before introducing himself to a new audience in "The Good Place."
He is currently starring in the hit Netflix show, "Man on the Inside," playing a retired professor who finds himself working as an undercover spy in a nursing home.

title: Singer Zach Top slams modern country music, says it lacks 'soul'
summary: Zach Top says modern country music sounds "perfect" and has lost its "soul," explaining why bluegrass and raw sounds are resonating with fans now.
story: Zach Top reveals how he plans on celebrating his CMAs win
Zach Top is sharing his hot take on modern country music, saying it now sounds "perfect" and lost some of its "soul."

During a recent interview with Rolling Stone, the 28-year-old country singer spoke about his new song, "Good Girls & Cowgirls," and why he thinks bluegrass music, which is what he started out playing, is now growing in popularity.

"From my perspective, it’s pretty parallel to the reason that my music is as popular as it is right now," he said. "We had a long time, at least in the country world — everything is really perfect and everything’s tuned. Everything’s pocketed just right. I think some of the soul got left behind in that."
In his opinion, people are now searching for music that is "a little more raw and real again," and that "bluegrass is only that" since when performing that genre, "there's nothing covering you up."
LUKE COMBS’ BRUTAL RESPONSE TO ‘LIBERAL’ LABELS: ‘WHY DO WE ALL CARE?’
Zach Top thinks modern country music has lost some of its "soul" because everything is too "perfect." (Taylor Hill/FilmMagic)

He explained that when playing bluegrass, "you better be a bada-- on your instrument and a bada-- singer," citing Tyler Childers and Zach Bryan as two other big country stars today who are embracing a "very real and raw" sound and finding great success with it.
"You’re not trying to chase perfection," he said. "You’re trying to just play good music and put your heart and soul into it. People enjoy that. And that’s what bluegrass has always been to me."
Top is known for playing traditional honky-tonk music and is credited as one of the younger country artists responsible for the resurgence of traditional country music.
He released his first EP in 2022, the same year he made his debut at the Grand Ole Opry. He had his big breakthrough in 2024, with the release of his debut album, "Cold Beer & Country Music."

Zach Top won CMA New Artist of the Year in 2025. (Michael Buckner/Billboard via Getty Images, File)

"I don't know. I brought a beer up on stage, read between the lines, you know," he said backstage at the CMAs about his celebration plans after the win.

"I got a bunch of my road crew here with me, my band. We're gonna go find someplace and knock a few beers back. I'll probably call my family at some point. … Outside of that, I just hope I can get to bed before 5 a.m., I suppose."
His latest song, "Good Girls & Cowgirls" debuts with its official release Aug. 21, along with another new song, "Other Side of Hurtin’."

Zach Top's latest song, "Good Girls & Cowgirls" debuts Aug. 21. (Taylor Hill/Getty Images, File)

BELLA HADID, KELSEA BALLERINI AND OTHER STARS KICK OFF SUMMER EARLY WITH BIKINI PHOTOS
Burke was photographed wearing a green swimsuit while in Malibu. (Michael Simon/GC Images)

title: Country star Waylon Wyatt says he nearly 'died' after sudden health crisis derailed his Grand Ole Opry debut

story: Chris Janson tells Fox News Digital he’s a ‘straight shootin’ country guy who wears his heart on his sleeve’ when discussing the importance of hunting, fishing and conservation.
Rising country music star Waylon Wyatt is recovering after a life-threatening battle with sepsis forced him to cancel several major career milestones.

In his latest video, Wyatt showed off his debut record, writing in his social media caption, "We shot this before I bout died but Dustpiles Vinyl are available to order now!! Get ‘em while they’re hot!"
Earlier this week, the 19-year-old singer shared a health update with fans, revealing he was discharged from a Montana hospital and is in Nashville seeking additional medical care.
MIRANDA LAMBERT SAYS SHE'S 'ADDICTED' TO SHOOTING GUNS ON HORSEBACK IN NEW WILD WEST HOBBY
The 19-year-old country singer revealed he's now in Nashville seeing specialists after being discharged from a Montana hospital. (Joseph Okpako/WireImage)

Wyatt shared multiple videos and photos during his hospitalization after a severe health scare. (Waylon Wyatt/Instagram)

title: Sammy Hagar buries decades-long feud with David Lee Roth after tour dates are axed
summary: Sammy Hagar posted an emotional video urging David Lee Roth to "carry on" and invited him to his Las Vegas residency after tour dates were axed.
story: Sammy Hagar doesn’t feel old yet and explains why he has no plans to retire.
David Lee Roth's summer comeback has hit an unexpected roadblock.
Several of the former Van Halen frontman's scheduled tour dates were abruptly canceled, prompting fans to wonder what caused the shake-up.
As news of the cancellations spread, Sammy Hagar wasted no time reaching out publicly to his longtime Van Halen counterpart with an emotional message of support.
SAMMY HAGAR ADMITS HE WOULDN’T BE AS ‘LEGENDARY’ WITHOUT VAN HALEN
Sammy Hagar and David Lee Roth during their tour in 2002. (SGranitz/WireImage)

"Hey Dave, Sammy here. I just got a call from Michael Anthony as I'm sitting down having my favorite cocktail, and I don't have to tell you what this is," Hagar said, smiling as he held up his signature margarita. "About your tour getting canceled.
"And I want to say from the bottom of my heart, I'm sorry. I hope you're well. I hope there's not a physical problem."
Shows in Colorado, Iowa, Kentucky and Illinois have all been canceled. No reason has been announced.

Only Roth's July dates have been scrapped. His five shows scheduled for August and September are still available for purchase through Ticketmaster, while his Aug. 7 performance in Sturgis, South Dakota, remains listed on his official website.
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
David Lee Roth and Sammy Hagar present the Best Rock Video award at the 2002 MTV Video Music Awards. (Kevin Kane/WireImage)

"Honestly, Mike and I love the fact that you've been out there doing it, supporting the greatest band in the world that we were both part of," Hagar said. "And, yeah, I'm really sorry. That's f---ed up. Supporting what we did in this band to keep this music alive."
He also reflected on the chemistry that made Van Halen one of rock's defining acts.
"You and I, Mikey, Al, Ed, cannot be replaced."
JON BON JOVI ABRUPTLY ENDS MADISON SQUARE GARDEN SHOW AFTER HEALTH SETBACK
Hagar then encouraged Roth to return whenever he's ready.
"So, when you're ready to carry on, you go, brother. Mike and I support you."
Hagar extended an open invitation for Roth to join him and Michael Anthony during their Las Vegas residency this September.
Rock musicians Michael Anthony, Sammy Hagar, Eddie Van Halen and Alex Van Halen pose for a portrait in 1986. (Paul Natkin/Getty Images)
"Come to Vegas for the residency in September. Come on, join us. Sing a couple songs, MC the damn show. Come out and just do what the f--- you do, which is pretty damn entertaining."
He closed the video with a heartfelt sendoff.
"Anyway, hope you're well. I really do. God bless, brother."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Hagar doubled down on the sentiment in the caption accompanying the video.

"I'm looking rough, but who cares I'm serious with this post. I hope the news about Dave is not AI!!!!! if it is, my post is still coming from my heart and soul. It is so important that this music carry on especially with the AI music out there. those of us that can still go out and play. should do it as long as they can physically and emotionally carry that torch. @vanhalen was, should be, and hopefully always will be real live music, not just for our fans, but for the future fans of real rock music."
The public support marked a notable turn for the two rock icons, whose relationship has long been defined by competition.
Roth and Hagar both worked the frontman for Van Halen at different times. (Fin Costello/Redferns)

After Roth exited Van Halen in 1985, Hagar stepped in as the band's new frontman alongside Eddie Van Halen, Alex Van Halen and Anthony. Hagar remained with the group until 1996 and later returned from 2003 to 2005. Roth reclaimed the mic full-time in 2006, remaining with Van Halen until the band's final chapter in 2020.

Though they each defined different eras of Van Halen, Hagar and Roth spent decades trading public jabs. They briefly joined forces for the 2002 "Song for Song, The Heavyweight Champs of Rock and Roll" tour, but the truce was short-lived as their rivalry quickly reignited.
The canceled dates mark another twist in Roth's return to live performance after he stunned fans by announcing his retirement in 2021.
"I am throwing in the shoes. I'm retiring," he told the Las Vegas Review-Journal. "This is the first, and only, official announcement."
His planned farewell Las Vegas residency was later scrapped amid COVID-19-related circumstances, but Roth ultimately returned to the stage in 2025 and continued to perform into 2026.

title: George Michael struggled with 'eternal conflict' over fame, Wham! bandmate Andrew Ridgeley says
summary: Andrew Ridgeley reveals George Michael's "eternal conflict" with fame, saying the Wham! singer created a character to fulfill his artistic destiny.
story: Andrew Ridgeley tells Fox News Digital about George Michael's complicated relationship with stardom, saying the singer created a public persona while wanting to live life as himself.

George Michael captivated millions with his chart-topping hits and powerhouse vocals, but, according to his Wham! bandmate, Andrew Ridgeley, the global superstar never truly embraced life in the spotlight.

In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, Ridgeley reflected on Michael's complicated relationship with fame ahead of the release of the documentary "WHAM! 10 Days In China," describing it as "an eternal conflict."

"He didn't want to be a star … in the sense of constantly projecting himself," Ridgeley said. "George Michael was a character that he created in order for him to fulfill his artistic destiny as a songwriter and a singer and a musician.
GEORGE MICHAEL DIED WORTH $128M, BUT FRIENDS SAY HE SECRETLY GAVE AWAY MILLIONS FOR DECADES: AUTHOR
This archival photograph shows Wham! members Andrew Ridgeley (left) and George Michael (right) posing on the Great Wall of China during the band's landmark 1985 visit to the country. (Neal Preston)
"But he wanted to live his life as Yog, you know, rather than as George Michael. There was always that conflict for him, and it was an eternal conflict, and one that he never fully resolved."
Known affectionately to friends as "Yog," Michael spent decades balancing worldwide fame with an intensely private personal life, a struggle Ridgeley believes many fans never fully understood.
"I don't think ... he was misunderstood," Ridgeley explained. "People weren't appraised of all the facts for a long time, you know, and he was a very, very private man."
If there was one thing audiences underestimated, Ridgeley said, it wasn't Michael's personality, it was the magnitude of his talent.
WATCH: WHAM! BAND MEMBER ANDREW RIDGELEY REVEALS WHAT FANS NEVER UNDERSTOOD ABOUT GEORGE MICHAEL

"People probably didn't understand the depth of his talent for a long time," he said. "That is bewildering and has always been bewildering ... If there's any misunderstanding, it was over the sheer scale of his talent."

The reflections are featured as part of "WHAM! 10 Days In China," a new documentary that revisits the duo's landmark 1985 concerts in Beijing and Guangzhou, which made Wham! the first Western pop group to perform in China.
Wham! members George Michael (right) and Andrew Ridgeley share a lighthearted moment inside a vehicle during the duo's landmark 1985 trip to China. (Neal Preston)

Drawing from newly restored archival footage, previously unseen material and firsthand interviews, the movie explores the band's groundbreaking visit while examining its cultural impact decades later.
Looking back more than 40 years after the historic performances, Ridgeley said one of the documentary's biggest revelations was finally uncovering the lasting legacy of the trip.
WATCH: WHAM! BAND MEMBER ANDREW RIDGELEY REVEALS THE UNTOLD STORY BEHIND THEIR TRIP TO CHINA IN 1985
OZZY OSBOURNE'S LEGENDARY FINAL PERFORMANCE RAISED A STAGGERING $190M FOR WORTHY CAUSES
"This is a retrospective which reveals as much as we possibly could about why we went, what we did, who were there and its legacy," Ridgeley told Fox News Digital.
"And its legacy was the most important aspect for me to try and discover because we knew nothing of it. The legacy in China remained unknown."
Although Michael famously criticized the band's first performance in China, Ridgeley said he wasn't surprised by his late friend's reaction.
Wham! band members visited China at the Great Wall in 1985. (Martyn Goddard)
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
"That wouldn't have been the first time he described a show as effing horrible," Ridgeley said with a laugh. "He didn't mince his words.

"I understood perfectly well why he felt that way," he continued. "But ... in hindsight, and as we discovered as part of this film, the legacy and the impact that those shows had on some people, especially, was life-changing."
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Michael died on Christmas Day in 2016 at age 53, but Ridgeley believes the singer would be deeply moved by the enduring admiration fans continue to show nearly a decade later.
"I think he would be very flattered by the depth of feeling that is held for him by how his memory has been honored, how his talent is recognized, how he is fêted and adored," Ridgeley said.
Andrew Ridgeley sits along the Great Wall of China during a return visit to the historic landmark decades after Wham!'s groundbreaking 1985 tour. (Craig Hastings)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"I think that that would have been very special to him, and he would have been very humbled by it."
"WHAM! 10 Days In China" premieres in theaters for a one-day-only release July 28.
Stephanie Giang-Paunon is an entertainment reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Bret Michaels hospitalized after 7-day medical ordeal left him playing through 'intense' pain
summary: Bret Michaels shared a hospital bed photo after a kidney stone procedure, revealing he played three concerts before the pain became too great.
story: Rock legend Bret Michaels talks about his new single, ‘Back in the Day,’ and discusses what sports and music means to him ahead of the 2023 Super Bowl.
Bret Michaels is sharing a health update with his fans after opening up about his issue with a kidney stone last weekend.
The 63-year-old musician took to Facebook July 22 to share with his followers that he is in recovery following a procedure to remove a kidney stone that would not pass on its own.

"On this #WisdomWednesday, the first thing I learned is complete gratitude for the frontline workers, doctors and nurses who this week have recently taken care of me, as the kidney stone (after almost 7 days of waiting it out) would not pass," he wrote.
JON BON JOVI ABRUPTLY ENDS MADISON SQUARE GARDEN SHOW AFTER HEALTH SETBACK
"The pain became intense but, as usual, I played through Charleston WV, Grantville PA and a special private show at Fairchild AFB in Spokane for veterans, active duty and their families."
The morning after playing the third concert in which he pushed through the pain, Michaels was admitted to a hospital because "the pain became too much when the stone would not pass."
Michaels shared a health update with his followers on Facebook, letting them know he had a procedure to remove a kidney stone. (Bret Michaels Facebook)
He then assured his followers "the operation has been done and is complete & I’m out of post-op recovery," and he hopes to be back on his feet as soon as possible.
"I’m doing everything within my power to feel better and continue playing great shows for great fans when I’ve got a complete clean bill of health," he said.
"Just want to say on this #WisdomWednesday that I am wise enough to know how important family, friends, fans, doctors and nurses play such a vital role in our everyday health."
In the photo shared on Facebook, the "Talk Dirty to Me" singer is lying in a hospital bed in an all-black outfit and a baseball cap with his body connected to monitors.
"Also just know, they eventually forced me out of my clothes & into a hospital gown lol as I had gone straight from the show to the hospital," he joked.

title: 'I Play Rocky' revives the gamble that made Sylvester Stallone a superstar
summary: The "I Play Rocky" trailer reveals how Sylvester Stallone refused massive paydays to star in his own screenplay, a gamble experts call unheard of.
story: The actor explained that his relationship with Stallone started off as professional since Stallone was his boss, but they developed a friendship.

Sylvester Stallone's historic "Rocky" story will be retold in Peter Farrelly's biographical drama, "I Play Rocky." To bring it to life, Farrelly had to flash back to how "Rocky" became a household name, and it started with Stallone selling his screenplay only if he was cast as the lead role.

In the "I Play Rocky" trailer, Stallone, played by Anthony Ippolito, presents the script that he wrote in three days to movie producers. They offered him outrageous amounts of money for the script, but Stallone wouldn't budge. Eventually, the producers gave in and cast Stallone in the role that changed his life.
Experts told Fox News Digital this move from Stallone was highly unheard of at the time.
Sylvester Stallone wrote "Rocky" in three days and refused to sell his screenplay unless he was cast as the lead role. (Getty Images)
"It was unheard of at the time, especially for someone in Stallone's economic situation, which was dire," film historian Dwight Cleveland said.
In the trailer, Stallone worked as a valet attendant when he created "Rocky."
SYLVESTER STALLONE REVEALS GRUELING ‘ROCKY’ PREP: ‘IF YOU WANT IT TO FEEL REAL, YOU HAVE TO LIVE IT’

Tisha Morris, entertainment attorney at Legacy Arts Law, said, "Stallone’s decision was extraordinarily unusual. Most first-time writers would have been expected to take the money and relinquish casting control."
From a legal standpoint, Stallone had every right to pull the move he did.

"Legally, Stallone could retain the screenplay and impose that condition because he owned the copyright," she continued. "However, the risk was whether the producers would simply walk away, leaving him with neither a sale nor a film. He was effectively betting the screenplay’s entire market value on himself as an actor."
Cleveland said Stallone acted just like his character in the movies when it came to the initial negotiations.

"Just like his character, Stallone had the confidence his story was a true winner, so he held his ground knowing that this was his shot at stardom both as an actor and as an author," he said. "He wasn't willing to give that up to someone else and be left without any clout in Hollywood. Film depicts the human condition and, in this case, it was true to the heart."
Talia Shire and Sylvester Stallone appear on a poster for "Rocky" in 1976. (Getty Images)

Marc Simon, entertainment attorney at Fox Rothschild in New York, told Fox News Digital Stallone's unwillingness to budge is one of the most-cited examples in Hollywood history of an unknown talent turning down life-changing money on principle.

"Stallone was an unknown actor with only minor bit parts to his name, and producers Robert Chartoff and Irwin Winkler wanted to buy his script outright — with reports indicating the offers escalated to $360,000 with stars (such as Ryan O'Neal, Burt Reynolds and James Caan) identified for the lead role," Simon said.
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"In monetary terms today, it’s probably the equivalent of someone being offered over $2 million. Stallone bet everything on starring in the film — a role that no one wanted him to play. He owned the property, and put it all on the line for his million-to-one shot, and like Rocky himself left an indelible mark on cinema and culture, which will be an everlasting legacy."
Beatrice Straight and Sylvester Stallone at the 49th Academy Awards in 1977. (Getty Images)
According to Simon, it was a win-win for producers to ultimately agree to Stallone's terms.

"Financially, Stallone's insistence on starring came paired with his willingness to accept a dramatically reduced salary and rights fee, which lowered the film's overall budget risk at a time when 'Rocky' was made on a modest budget of roughly $1 million," he said. "So, the economics became more palatable to a studio like United Artists that was otherwise wary of an unknown actor carrying the film."

Released in 1976, "Rocky" became one of the biggest underdog success stories in Hollywood history. The movie follows small-time Philadelphia boxer Rocky Balboa as he gets the once-in-a-lifetime chance to fight heavyweight champion Apollo Creed.
Sylvester Stallone on the set of his movie "Rocky II." (Sunset Boulevard/Corbis via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Made on a modest budget, Rocky was both a critical and commercial hit, earning 10 Academy Award nominations (including Best Actor and Best Original Screenplay for Stallone) and winning three Oscars for Best Picture, Best Director for John G. Avildsen and Best Film Editing.
"Rocky" went on to launch one of cinema's most successful franchises and cemented Rocky Balboa as one of the most iconic characters in movie history.
Sylvester Stallone became a household name thanks to the "Rocky" franchise. (Getty Images)

Amazon is gearing up to release "I Play Rocky" in November. According to reports, Stallone is not involved in the biopic. Speaking to The Playlist, Stallone said, "I was shocked to read [about] it. I have zero to do with it."
Ippolito will star as Stallone, and AnnaSophia Robb will play Sasha Czack, Stallone's first wife. Other members of the cast include: Stephan James, Matt Dillon and P.J. Byrne.

title: 'Baywatch: Hawaii' star Brandy Ledford says she 'wanted to truly check out' before rehab saved her life
summary: Brandy Ledford shares how substance abuse nearly destroyed her before rehab and why connecting with fans on Passes is part of her journey in building close connections.
story: The actress, now a wellness advocate and content creator at Passes, shares how trusting God, connecting with her ‘sober sisters’ and telling her story changed her life after rehab.
Brandy Ledford has plenty of reasons to celebrate these days.
The actress, who made hearts race as lifeguard Dawn Masterton on "Baywatch: Hawaii," recently marked 14 years of sobriety.
Today, the 57-year-old is a wellness advocate, yoga teacher and creator on Passes, where she shares exclusive content and connects directly with fans.
But before she found peace, Ledford said she reached her breaking point.
CARA DELEVINGNE ADMITS SHE USED PARTY DRUG GHB DAILY BEFORE TERRIFYING SEIZURES FORCED HER SOBER
"Baywatch: Hawaii" alum Brandy Ledford, now a content creator on Passes, spoke to Fox News Digital about her sobriety journey. (Caroline Malouf)

"There was a moment when I realized something had to change in my life," Ledford told Fox News Digital. "I definitely was abusing substances to avoid my feelings. And I was doing it in a way that was really harmful to me, to my mental health and to my family. And I had a harrowing last night before I checked myself into rehab.
"I didn't know there was going to be a way out."
Brandy Ledford is seen here as Dawn Masterton in "Baywatch: Hawaii." (ZUMA Press Inc./ALAMY)
Ledford said addiction ultimately left her feeling trapped, hopeless and convinced nothing could numb her pain.
WATCH: ‘BAYWATCH’ STAR BRANDY LEDFORD SAYS FAITH HELPED TRANSFORM HER SOBRIETY JOURNEY

"I didn't feel like there was a way out," she shared. "Drinking didn't solve my problems. I was addicted to prescription pain medication. [That] didn't solve my problems. And, in the end, it didn't really take away any of the things I didn't want to be feeling. And that was my last hope. And when I figured that that didn't work anymore, I really just wanted to truly check out because I didn't see a way out."
Brandy Ledford starred in the 2000 television series "Andromeda" opposite Kevin Sorbo. (Fireworks Entertainment/Album/Alamy)

Ledford previously told Basic magazine she struggled with alcohol and drug addiction for much of her life. According to the outlet, she began smoking marijuana at age 11 and was using cocaine and drinking alcohol by age 14. Ledford was jailed twice on alcohol-related charges before turning 17 and developed a cocaine addiction by 18.
Years later, Ledford said she reached a turning point after what she described as "a really horrible last night," the moment she realized something had to change.
Brandy Ledford attends the Silver Spoon Beauty Buffet sponsored by Allure on Day 1 in 2003. (WireImage for Silver Spoon (formerly The Cabana))
"The next day, I checked myself into rehab and found the way out," she said.
Ledford said the greatest gift sobriety gave her wasn't the one she expected. Instead, she found something she never knew she was missing.
Brandy Ledford attends the 6th Jam For Janie Grammy Awards Viewing Party presented by Live Nation at the Hollywood Palladium in Los Angeles Feb. 2, 2025. (Getty Images for Janie's Fund)

"The friendships," she said, fighting back tears. "I didn’t know that I would find my best friends in sobriety. I have a really solid network of girlfriends I've had for 40 years, and they’re here in my life. I made a couple of friends in sobriety who are my lifelines.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Hilary Roberts (left) and Brandy Ledford arrive at the 33rd Annual Race To Erase MS Gala at Fairmont Century Plaza in Los Angeles June 5, 2026. (Steve Granitz/FilmMagic)

"I didn't expect the friendships," she said. "I didn't know that was a possibility. Then I found the community and the network of sober sisters who really support each other and lift each other through everything we go through. I didn't expect my life would be perfect. I never thought, 'Oh good, now I'm sober, everything's going to line up.' But I do know that if I stay sober, eventually things line up. And I learned that from the really brave women in this recovery program."
Brandy Ledford's movie debut came with a memorable role in "Demolition Man" alongside Sylvester Stallone. (JC Olivera/Getty Images)
Ledford once kept her addiction struggles private. Today, she's sharing her story in hopes of inspiring others to seek recovery while leaning on her faith in God every step of the way.
The actress said sharing her recovery journey has become one of the most meaningful parts of her life.

Friendly House Board member Brandy Ledford speaks onstage during Friendly House's 33rd Annual Awards Luncheon at The Beverly Hilton in Beverly Hills, on Oct. 28, 2023. (Getty Images for Friendly House)

"It really is one day at a time," she said. "I give a lot of credit to my higher power, my God, because I couldn't do it without God's help. I have a strong faith. I also didn't expect people to want to hear from somebody in the public about their sobriety. I didn't expect so many people to talk to me about my sobriety and be helped by my story. And what I love about that is I'm able to share my experience so that my experience wasn't wasted.

"I went through a lot, a lot of really challenging, tough times," she said. "And the fact that I can use that now to help others and create strength and hope in others — and in myself — is such a gift of sobriety. It's such a way to keep us sober, to share our stories. But I never really expected people wanted to hear what I had to say.
Brandy Ledford and Carmen Electra attend the 33rd Annual Race To Erase MS Gala at Fairmont Century Plaza in Los Angeles June 5, 2026. (Getty Images for Race to Erase MS)

"I didn't expect to ever talk about that in a public way. And I'm so proud to do so. I'm so proud to be able to help others and just share my truth, my story. And I'm not ashamed of it. I just want to shine a light on how good your life can get when you can be free of addiction."
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Brandy Ledford told Fox News Digital she continues to lean on her personal relationship with God. (Matt Kallish)
Ledford said sobriety didn't just transform her life. It also strengthened her relationship with God.

"My relationship with God has helped shape this new chapter in my life by listening to His will, by turning my will and my life over to God," she said. "Any time I have a decision to make, I lean on my faith to help me find the answers. I pause instead of making rash decisions, and ... I have even more trust that the answers will come.
Brandy Ledford attends the 30th anniversary of "Baywatch" at the Viceroy Hotel in Santa Monica, Calif., Sept. 24, 2019. (Presley Ann/Getty Images)

"There's an expression: 'Trust God, clean house,'" she beamed. "I didn't know that before I got sober, but I always talked about how much faith I had. Faith and trust are so different, and it's such a layered concept."
Brandy Ledford attends the premiere of ABC News Studios docuseries "After Baywatch: Moment in the Sun" at The Bungalow on Aug. 26, 2024, in Santa Monica, Calif. (Variety via Getty Images)
Ledford said she has developed a deeper understanding of her relationship with God by learning to trust Him while remaining true to herself.
The desire to connect with others has also shaped Ledford’s latest venture. As a creator on Passes, she said the platform allows her to build meaningful relationships with fans on her own terms.
Brandy Ledford splits her time between Los Angeles, Vancouver and Kauai. (Amanda Edwards/Getty Images)
The site lets celebrities, athletes and digital creators share content and interact directly with subscribers.
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP
Today, Brandy Ledford is also a wellness advocate. (Courtesy of Brandy Ledford)

"I don't answer my DMs on Instagram, TikTok or Twitter (now X) only because I get a lot of them," she said. "It's not personal. But in this way, I feel like I get to have a relationship with fans, and they get to know the real me.

"I get to really connect on a one-on-one level, but I also get to be my full self and benefit from it, benefit from being who I want to be without somebody dictating how they think it should be. And it's fun. It's a really fun way to share my life with others and connect.
Brandy Ledford stays in shape as a yoga teacher. (Presley Ann/Getty Images for Baby2Baby)

"My whole idea of connection is the opposite of addiction," she said. "And to be able to connect with people in a one-on-one way and to really be free to do so, it's kind of brilliant. I love this new world, with us getting to be in control, getting to be in charge and still being super creative."

These days, Ledford is embracing a new chapter. In addition to doing voiceover work for "King of the Hill," she serves on the board of the Red Songbird Foundation, a nonprofit founded in 2009 by singer Hilary Roberts, who has been sober from drugs and alcohol since 1997. The organization provides support for people struggling with trauma, mental health challenges, substance abuse disorder and PTSD.
Brandy Ledford hopes her story will inspire others struggling to turn their lives around. (Matt Kallish)
"I'm really proud to be in a position where I can do things that help others," Ledford said. "I just want to continue."
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Meghan Markle's 'MasterChef Australia' controversy may be exactly the point: experts
summary: Meghan Markle's "MasterChef Australia" guest judge role sparks boycott calls and praise as royal experts debate whether the appearance can reset her brand.
story: Royal broadcaster Neil Sean discusses an interview given by Angela Kelly, Queen Elizabeths long-time dresser and best friend regarding conflicts within the palace including tension surrounding Meghan Markle and Prince Harrys wedding.
Meghan Markle's upcoming appearance on "MasterChef Australia" has already sparked debate, with royal experts telling Fox News Digital the backlash may be just as important as the episode itself.

The hit reality cooking series announced in an Instagram post that the 44-year-old Duchess of Sussex would be joining the show as a guest judge for Sunday's episode, writing that Markle will be "bringing her love of food, entertaining and seasonal produce to one of the competition's most memorable challenges."
In a press release, Markle, who filmed the episode during her visit to Australia with her husband Prince Harry in April, explained why she wanted to take part in the episode.
'MASTERCHEF' FINALIST SAYS BUSY FAMILIES ARE LOSING SOMETHING MORE IMPORTANT THAN HOME-COOKED MEALS
"What attracted me to the MasterChef Australia kitchen? Two things: my love of food and my love of Australia. It was an easy yes," Markle said.
Meghan Markle's upcoming role as a guest judge on "MasterChef Australia" sparked praise and backlash.  (Getty Images)
"It’s such a great show," she continued. "I’m just really honored that I was asked to be able to be here with you and to be able to judge some of these meals."
The press release noted that the cooks will take on the challenge of creating "a dish fit for a Duchess" using some of Markle's "favorite seasonal ingredients."
MEGHAN MARKLE'S SHOW EMMY NOMINATION 'SOMEWHAT BAFFLING' DUE TO LACKLUSTER RATINGS: EXPERT
In a preview of the episode that appeared on Sydney's 10 News, Markle appeared alongside season 18 "MasterChef Australia" judges Poh Ling Yeow, Sofia Levin and Jean-Christophe Novelli.
Markle introduced her chosen ingredients, noting that the chefs had "quite the bounty her" and proudly sharing that her children Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, "eat Brussels sprouts."
"That’s impressive," Levin said.
PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE’S HOLLYWOOD DREAMS HIT WALL AS EXPERT WARNS OF ‘TOXIC BRAND’ STIGMA

"Food and cooking to me is really a love language," Markle explained later in the preview. "I think it’s such a great way to connect. It’s something that can feel sentimental and meaningful and It’s how I, it’s how I show my nurturing and love for my friends, family, and my kids."
The duchess will appear in Sunday's episode of the cooking competition show.  (Netflix)

Following the announcement, Markle's participation in "MasterChef Australia" was quickly met with a divided reaction on social media, earning both praise from supporters and calls for a boycott from critics.
"Why? She’s not a chef??? Not interested!" one Instagram user wrote.
"Can't stand her. She's not a chef," another agreed, adding, "Why is she even on this show."
"Thanks for the heads-up and making it easier to avoid," one critic commented as another chimed in, "Definitely won't watch it!"
"First time since the beginning of this show, that I WON’T be watching, first time!!" another detractor wrote.
Markle recently earned her first Daytime Emmy Award nomination for "With Love, Meghan." (Jake Rosenberg/Netflix © 2025)
However, others expressed their excitement over seeing Markle's appearance.
"Can’t wait to watch it!!!" one social media user commented.
"I'll be WATCHING!!" another added.
"I know she will do a great job," a fan enthused.
"I CAN'T WAIT!! WE LOVE YOU PRINCESS MEGHAN," another supporter wrote.
"I love this for her… she is working and finding opportunities for herself," one fan added.
"All the people saying they won’t watch are the first ones who will be watching and later criticizing," another commenter wrote. "I can’t wait to watch! Love Meghan!"
Markle's appearance also made headlines and fueled debate online after a report claimed her team requested that she not be referred to as "royalty" during filming.
Royal expert Richard Fitzwilliam said the controversy around her appearance could be exactly the point.  (Netflix)
The polarized reaction to Markle's latest gig underscores a familiar pattern for the Duchess of Sussex, whose post-royal ventures have often generated as much controversy as publicity.

Royal expert Richard Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital the attention surrounding Markle's appearance, whether positive or negative, could ultimately benefit both the duchess and the cooking competition.
"Every time Meghan’s name gets in the papers, even if it is negative, it builds up the power of her brand," he said. "It also helps to hype the show before it starts."
"She was chosen as a guest judge to boost the ratings of the show," Fitzwilliams added.

While Markle's role has prompted questions about her qualifications, British broadcaster Helena Chard argued that professional cooking experience isn't necessarily a requirement for a celebrity guest judge.
"I don’t believe she’s a qualified chef. But then, they’ve had Steve Irwin as a guest judge before and he wasn’t a chef either," she pointed out. "So it’s not really about culinary credentials."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

The "Suits" alum's guest judging stint marks her latest foray into the food and lifestyle world. In March 2025, Markle's "With Love, Meghan" lifestyle and reality show premiered on Netflix. In the show, Meghan shared cooking, gardening and entertaining tips alongside celebrity guests. "With Love, Meghan" also served as a launchpad for her As Ever lifestyle brand.

In January 2026, Netflix reportedly canceled the show after two seasons and later announced that it was ending its partnership with the As Ever brand though Markle and Prince Harry retained a first-look production deal with the streamer. However, "With Love, Meghan" recently received a surprise Daytime Emmy Award nomination for outstanding lifestyle series. "Meghan does have an interest in food and entertaining," Chard noted. "So from a PR perspective, appearing on ‘MasterChef Australia’ alongside well-known hosts, strengthens her brand."
Fitzwilliams argued that Markle's involvement could boost ratings.  (Netflix)

While Chard saw the guest judging role as a natural fit, other royal experts told Fox News Digital that the response illustrates the challenges Markle continues to face with public perception after stepping away from royal life.

"People are talking more about why she's judging than what she's judging," royal reporter Kinsey Schofield said. "An image reset only works if the audience buys into the new image, and right now many viewers still see a disconnect between Meghan's branding and her actual experience or authority in this space."

"Social media always amplifies the loudest voices," the "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered" host continued. "That said, there does seem to be a broader sense of Meghan fatigue. Every project arrives carrying years of baggage, and that's a challenge most celebrities simply don't have. She isn't launching from a blank slate. She's launching from a very divided public reputation."
Fitzwilliams agreed, saying there have been "sufferers from Meghan fatigue for some time" and that "a great many viewers feel this way."

"Lifestyle is aspirational, it's lucrative, and it gives celebrities tremendous control over their image," Schofield said. "The problem is that audiences don't just buy recipes or table settings anymore. They're buying authenticity."
Other experts warned that the appearance could "backfire." (Netflix)
Fitzwilliams shared his view that Markle's cameo is also tied to her broader business ambitions. "She is returning to food in the hope this boosts sales of the As Ever products," he said.
Schofield said that the guest judge appearance may not deliver the hoped-for results, arguing that every project that Markle takes on is now judged through the lens of the duchess herself.

"Meghan has had several opportunities to reinvent herself since leaving royal life, and the pattern has remained the same… enormous publicity followed by polarized reactions," she told Fox News Digital. "One television appearance probably won't rewrite that narrative overnight."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"People often react to the brand before they react to the product," she added. "That's the downside of building such a personality-driven business model. Every project becomes less about the content itself and more about whether people have bought into Meghan as the person selling it."
Experts questioned whether audiences would see Markle as a credible judge of the contestants' dishes.  (Getty Images)
Beyond the public reaction, some royal experts questioned whether audiences would view her as a credible choice to critique contestants on "MasterChef Australia."

"Celebrity guest judges aren't expected to have Michelin stars, but they do need to bring something credible to the table," Schofield said. "Meghan's challenge is that she's still trying to establish herself as an authority in this space while much of the audience sees her as someone playing a part."
Royal expert Hilary Fordwich shared her opinion that Markle's divisive public image makes her guest appearance different from most casting decisions.

"Meghan is so polarizing that while such an appearance would be low-risk for any regular celebrity, it is likely to backfire," she said, adding that the duchess "has no credentials" and "doesn't come across as authentic."
"Given the failure of her previous cooking attempts, with lackluster ratings, this is all she can do now which is to be involved in a show which is already a success," Fordwich said.

Meghan, Duchess of Sussex is pictured at the Hubb Community Kitchen in London on Nov. 21, 2018 to celebrate the success of their cookbook. The kitchen was set up by women affected by the Grenfell tower fire, and the duchess wrote a foreword to the cookbook to help raise funds for the victims. (POOL/AFP via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
However, royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner shared a more optimistic outlook on Markle's latest endeavor.

"Meghan is a master at reinventions, keeping herself in the public eye, and ‘MasterChef Australia’ is the latest platform to succumb to the real values of the lady and obviously cooking is one of many talents," he said.

Turner pointed to Markle's previous charitable work with the Hubb Community Kitchen, which was established in the wake of London's devastating Grenfell Tower fire. In June 2017, a fire ignited in the 24-story Grenfell Tower apartment block which killed 72 people and displaced hundreds of residents. After becoming involved with the community kitchen in 2018, Markle cooked alongside local women and helped publish a charity cookbook that raised money to support the initiative.
The royal expert told Fox News Digital that he also believed Markle would resonate with Australian audiences.
"Australia is a country which values people who have initiative and drive, and Meghan has that people's touch to support and offer cookery as one of her skill bases," he said.
Royal expert Ian Pelham Turner said Markle is a "master at reinventions." (Netflix)
For all the debate surrounding Markle's guest judging role, experts said the real question is whether the attention translates into viewers.
Schofield believes Markle's appearance could prove beneficial for "MasterChef Australia" if the buzz prompts audiences to tune in.

"Meghan guarantees headlines, and headlines translate into curiosity," she said. "Whether that curiosity becomes ratings or resentment is the million-dollar question. Producers know controversy can be good for television, but only if viewers stay for the episode instead of switching it off."
Ashley Hume is an entertainment journalist for Fox News Digital and Fox Business who covers breaking news, celebrity culture, major industry events and the business of entertainment.

story: Patty Morin responds to video of actress Selena Gomez crying over deportations on 'Fox & Friends Weekend'.

Gomez is enjoying a relaxing vacation with her husband, during which she posed in various swimsuit. (Selena Gomez Instagram)
SYDNEY SWEENEY SHARES BIKINI AND UNDERWEAR PHOTOS IN INSTAGRAM DUMP FROM AUSTRALIA TRIP

Gomez wore a white one-piece bathing suit while playing Scrabble with her husband. (Selena Gomez Instagram)

title: Financial hardship may age the brain faster, researchers say in new study
summary: Chronic poverty over decades was linked to memory loss, slower processing speed and brain shrinkage, with strongest effects among men and APOE-ε4 carriers.
story: Sleep is critical for brain function and longevity, according to Dr. Daniel Amen, psychiatrist and owner of Amen Clinics in California.
Adults who faced persistent financial hardship showed poorer cognitive performance and signs of accelerated brain aging later in life, according to a new study.
Researchers at University College London looked at 2,759 U.K. participants from the MRC National Survey of Health and Development born in 1946, as stated in a press release.
Adults who reported experiencing persistent financial hardship or low income performed worse on cognitive tests that assessed verbal memory and processing speed.
LONGER LIVES, WORSE HEALTH? SCIENTISTS UNCOVER TROUBLING TREND ACROSS GENERATIONS
Those who had persistent low income also showed poorer brain health based on MRI scans, which measured markers of aging like brain shrinkage and enlarged ventricles.
Adults who faced persistent financial hardship showed poorer cognitive performance and signs of accelerated brain aging later in life, according to a new study. (iStock)

"[While] we know well that cognitive decline is associated with both genetic risks and adverse childhood experience, we knew very little about what happens during the life course … particularly, the experience of persistent financial stress over the lifetime," study author Dr Jacques Wels from the Unit for Lifelong Health & Ageing at UCL told Fox News Digital.
ALZHEIMER'S BLOOD TESTS MAY PREDICT SYMPTOMS YEARS IN ADVANCE, BUT EXPERTS URGE CAUTION

"The study clearly demonstrates … that the accumulation of poverty is linked to cognitive decline. We used different measures of lifecourse financial adversity and different measures of cognitive decline and they all show the same results, which makes the results solid."
Participants who reported experiencing persistent financial hardship or low income performed worse on cognitive tests that assessed verbal memory and processing speed. (iStock)
The associations were strongest among men, people who had disadvantaged childhoods and carriers of the APOE-ε4 genetic variant that is linked to a higher risk of Alzheimer's disease.

"The study shows that [while] cognitive decline is both a matter of genetic risks and individual behaviors, it is also affected by the experiences we live over our lives that we don’t always have control on," Wels added.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Based on the findings, the researchers suggested that chronic financial adversity over decades, rather than short-term periods of hardship, is linked to faster cognitive aging.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
This could be the result of chronic stress leading to inflammation or increased cognitive load from persistent financial worry, the authors proposed.
There were some limitations of the study, including that its observational design could not prove that the financial stress caused the cognitive effects.
Those who had persistent low income also showed poorer brain health based on MRI scans, which measured markers of aging like brain shrinkage and enlarged ventricles. (iStock)

"We are looking at a cohort of people born in 1946 – so their life course experience is really dependent on the context they lived in," Wels noted. "For instance, we found stronger effects among males, which reflects the ‘breadwinner’ role of men in older cohorts, something we might not observe in more recent generations."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Even after accounting for many other factors that could influence brain health, it's still possible that unmeasured variables may have affected the results, the study authors acknowledged.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

While reducing long-term poverty could help protect brain health, the UCL team said further studies are needed to determine whether improving financial circumstances directly reduces the risk of cognitive decline and dementia.
