title: This red state is strengthening its grip as America's next economic heavyweight
summary: IRS migration data reveal over $5 billion in wealth flowing into Texas as Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston and Austin fuel the state's population boom.
story: Gabriela von zur Muehlen, chief policy officer at the Texas Association of Business, says Texas’ low costs and strong supply chains help attract billionaires, CEOs and manufacturers.
The race to become America's next economic heavyweight may already have a frontrunner.

The latest Internal Revenue Service (IRS) migration data show billions of dollars in taxpayer wealth flowing into Texas, while Census figures show the state's largest metropolitan areas continue to outpace much of the country in population growth, strengthening a decades-long shift in America's economic center of gravity.

What's more, Texas isn't relying on a single boomtown. Dallas-Fort Worth added more residents than any metropolitan area in the country over the past year, while Houston, Austin and San Antonio also ranked among the nation's fastest-growing metros.

That unusual breadth gives Texas multiple engines of economic growth, providing businesses with larger labor pools, diversified industries and a broader customer base than states anchored by a single dominant city.
Critics have argued that Texas' economic success is mostly a numbers game. But the latest federal data suggest there's more to it. (Mike Lawrie/WireImage/GettyImages)
BILLIONS IN TAXPAYER INCOME ARE LEAVING TWO ICONIC STATES — AS A NEW ECONOMIC MAP EMERGES

The population boom has been accompanied by an influx of wealth. IRS migration data analyzed by the Tax Foundation show the Lone Star State gained more than $5 billion in adjusted gross income from interstate movers, while California and New York recorded multibillion-dollar losses.

"Capital follows where there is confidence," Texas Association of Business Chief Policy Officer Gabriela von zur Muehlen previously told Fox News Digital. "And right now there is a tremendous amount of confidence in Texas."
Von zur Muehlen said Texas' tax structure and predictable regulatory environment continue to attract businesses and investment from other states, helping reinforce the state's economic momentum.

While Florida attracted the nation's largest influx of taxpayer wealth and South Carolina posted the strongest inbound migration rate, Texas stood out by combining billions in new taxable income with rapid growth across Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston, Austin and San Antonio.

Economists say that combination matters because higher-income households bring spending, investment, entrepreneurship and tax revenue that can accelerate job creation, fuel commercial development and attract even more businesses. Over time, those forces can transform fast-growing metros into some of the nation's most influential economic hubs.
ONE SOUTHERN CITY YOU'VE NEVER HEARD OF IS GROWING FASTER THAN ANYWHERE ELSE IN AMERICA

Unlike simple population counts, adjusted gross income offers a glimpse into the economic resources newcomers bring with them. Higher-income households can contribute disproportionately to consumer spending, investment and local tax collections, making income migration an important measure of a region's long-term economic strength.
The migration data are only part of the story.

Earlier federal estimates showed Texas wasn't just adding residents — it was becoming wealthier on a per-person basis. Despite adding roughly 419,000 residents in 2025, more than any other state, Texas' economic output climbed to about $2.9 trillion, while per-capita GDP continued to rise, suggesting the state's economy was becoming more productive rather than simply larger.
THE RED STATES RACING AHEAD IN AMERICA'S POWERFUL WEALTH BOOM — AND THE STATES FALLING BEHIND
As businesses leave high-cost states, Texas has become the undisputed top destination. (Tom Fox/The Dallas Morning News/Getty Images)

Business leaders say those trends are creating a self-reinforcing cycle. As more workers and higher-income households relocate to Texas, companies gain access to a larger labor pool and customer base, encouraging additional hiring, investment and expansion. That growth, in turn, creates more jobs and opportunities that can attract even more residents.

The migration has coincided with years of corporate relocations and business investment across the state, particularly in technology, finance, manufacturing and energy. The influx has also fueled new housing developments, logistics hubs, manufacturing projects and expanding commercial corridors across many of Texas' fastest-growing metropolitan areas.

Supporters of Texas' economic model argue its lack of a state income tax, relatively affordable cost of living and business-friendly climate continue attracting both employers and workers, reinforcing the state's long-term growth.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
California and New York remain among the nation's largest and most influential economies.

But the latest Census, IRS and federal economic data suggest Texas continues gaining ground by attracting people, taxpayer wealth and economic output simultaneously, an uncommon combination that could reshape where businesses invest, jobs are created, and economic influence grows over the coming decade.
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: Everyday Revolutionary War heroes take center stage in Trump's 'Spirit of '76' exhibit
summary: The Caesar Rodney statue and 22 other installations at Freedom Plaza honor common, everyday Revolutionary War heroes as part of America's 250th anniversary under President Trump.
story: Fox News Digital gets an exclusive guided tour of the 'Spirit of '76' exhibit with designer Matthew Taylor, who shares the stories of some overlooked Revolutionary War heroes and Caesar Rodney's legendary midnight ride.

EXCLUSIVE: Beneath a towering 23-foot bronze figure holding the Declaration of Independence aloft, designer Matthew Taylor stopped beside an equestrian statue that many Americans have likely never seen, or even heard of.

"Most Americans have never heard of Caesar Rodney," Taylor told Fox News Digital during an exclusive tour of the new Spirit of '76 exhibition at Freedom Plaza. "But we owe this man an enormous debt of gratitude."

The temporary installation, unveiled as part of America's 250th anniversary celebration, transforms Freedom Plaza into an open-air gallery honoring Revolutionary War figures whose names rarely appear in history textbooks.

Commissioned by President Donald Trump, the exhibition features 22 statues and sculptural installations, including a restored equestrian monument of Rodney, a towering "Spirit of Liberty" centerpiece, bronze figures representing Revolutionary soldiers, and an immersive memorial honoring Americans who died aboard British prison ships during the Revolution.
EXPERTS FINALLY SOLVE MYSTERY OF TEENAGE REVOLUTIONARY WAR SOLDIER 246 YEARS AFTER HIS DEATH
Matthew Taylor stands beneath the Caesar Rodney statue with members of the fabrication team during the opening of the Spirit of '76 exhibition at Freedom Plaza. (Dan Fleuette)

According to the National Park Service, the exhibit was created to honor the "heroes and martyrs of the Revolution" during America's semiquincentennial and is intended to celebrate the enduring "Spirit of '76' that continues to live on in every American heart."
The centerpiece installations include the Caesar Rodney equestrian statue, the "12 Soldiers of the Revolution," the Prison Ship Martyrs memorial and the 23-foot Spirit of Liberty statue.
ARCHAEOLOGICAL DIG AT BATTLE OF BUNKER HILL SITE UNCOVERS REVOLUTIONARY WAR ARTIFACTS
The restored Caesar Rodney equestrian statue stands at Freedom Plaza during the opening of the Spirit of '76 exhibition in Washington, D.C. (Dan Fleuette)
Rather than beginning with George Washington or Thomas Jefferson, however, Taylor chose to introduce visitors to Rodney.

The Delaware statesman, one of the signers of the Declaration of Independence, is remembered for his legendary overnight ride from Dover to Philadelphia in July 1776. Suffering from severe illness, Rodney rode roughly 80 miles through a storm to cast the vote that broke Delaware's deadlock in favor of independence.

"Of all the signers of the Declaration of Independence, Caesar Rodney is one of the most exciting," Taylor said. "When Delaware's delegation was deadlocked, he rode through the night to cast the vote that helped secure American independence."
THE REVOLUTIONARY LANDMARKS WHERE WASHINGTON, ADAMS AND JEFFERSON CHANGED AMERICA
A welder from Atelier Missor places final touches on the "Spirit of Liberty" statue before the installation was made public earlier this month. (Dan Fleuette)

For decades, the bronze statue stood in Wilmington's Rodney Square before being removed in 2020. It now occupies one of the most prominent locations in the nation's capital, just blocks from both the White House and the Capitol.
From Rodney's ride, Taylor naturally guides visitors into the next chapter of the American story.

Arranged around the plaza are bronze sculptures representing 12 Revolutionary War soldiers. Rather than depicting famous generals, the statues celebrate ordinary Americans whose individual stories reflect the sacrifices of the Revolutionary generation.
"These are ordinary citizens who did extraordinary things," Taylor said. "Every one of these statues tells the story of someone who answered the call during the Revolution."

An inscription featuring a quote from George Washington appears on the base of the Spirit of Liberty statue at Freedom Plaza in Washington, D.C., during America's 250th anniversary celebration. (Dan Fleuette)

Among them is Samuel Whittemore, who fought British troops at age 78. According to Taylor, Whittemore was bayoneted multiple times, shot in the head and left for dead before surviving and living into his 90s.
Another figure, Simon Knowles, enlisted at just 15 years old and served alongside George Washington throughout much of the Revolutionary War before returning home to live as a farmer.
Taylor said those stories represent the exhibition's central message.
"Unlike monuments to George Washington or Thomas Jefferson, these statues honor ordinary Americans who did extraordinary things," he said.
Nearby, another installation tells one of the Revolution's lesser-known tragedies.

Designed as visitors physically walk through its narrow bronze panels, the Prison Ship Martyrs memorial recreates the outline of a British prison ship. According to the National Park Service, nearly 12,000 Americans died aboard prison ships during the Revolutionary War; even more than were killed in combat during the conflict.
Taylor said the memorial is meant to immerse visitors in that experience.
"As you walk inside, you hear the water from the fountain," he explained during the tour. "It helps place you inside the story."

The fountain itself has also become part of the experience. Taylor noted it was recently restored to operation after years of sitting idle, providing the soundscape surrounding the memorial while complementing the plaza's redesign.
The Prison Ship Martyrs memorial at Freedom Plaza honors Americans who died aboard British prison ships during the Revolutionary War. (Dan Fleuette)
Towering above the entire exhibition stands the Spirit of Liberty, a new bronze figure inspired by iconic American monuments while looking toward the country's next 250 years.

Standing 23 feet tall, the statue holds an exact bronze replica of the Declaration of Independence in one hand while raising a sword skyward with the other. Around its base are reliefs depicting three defining moments of the Revolution: the signing of the Declaration of Independence, George Washington crossing the Delaware River and the British surrender at Yorktown.
"The Spirit of Liberty represents the sacrifices that gave birth to this nation," Taylor said.

During Fox News Digital's visit, visitors gathered around the plaza to photograph the statues against the Washington skyline. Low-angle views of the bronze figures framed them against bright summer skies, while Rodney's horse appeared frozen mid-stride as though continuing the historic ride that helped shape the nation's founding.
For Taylor, whose career has largely been spent both behind the camera and behind the scenes designing historical works, the exhibition is about more than commemorating famous names.
Instead, he hopes visitors leave thinking about people they had never encountered before arriving at Freedom Plaza.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"When visitors leave here," Taylor said, "I hope they realize they can do extraordinary things themselves. America was built by ordinary citizens who answered extraordinary moments."
The Spirit of '76 exhibition is free to the public and is scheduled to remain on display throughout the nation's 250th anniversary celebration.
Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

title: Fauci's newly released COVID diaries reveal bizarre fixation on fame as pandemic deaths mounted
summary: Anthony Fauci's private diary entries reveal he called himself the most famous person in the country while documenting rising COVID-19 death tolls.
story: Senator Rand Paul forecasts Dr. Anthony Fauci's dishonesty in his upcoming Senate testimony regarding COVID-19 origins. Paul provides evidence of Fauci destroying records and actively funding dangerous gain-of-function research in Wuhan, China. He asserts that Fauci's support for such risky research, despite the potential for a pandemic, represents ‘the worst public health decision’ made in our lifetime.
Newly released diary entries reveal that as COVID-19 deaths mounted around the world, former White House COVID advisor Dr. Anthony Fauci became increasingly fixated on his newfound celebrity.

Released by Senate Homeland Security Committee Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., the journals chronicle Fauci's day-to-day role during the COVID-19 crisis through conversations with President Donald Trump, governors and world leaders, media appearances, and his personal observations as the pandemic unfolded.

Paul, a longtime Fauci critic who frequently clashed with Fauci over the federal response and the origins of the virus, made the diaries public as part of the committee's ongoing oversight investigation. The release comes days before Fauci is scheduled to testify before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee after being subpoenaed by Paul.
GABBARD SAYS DECLASSIFIED BIOLAB RECORDS VALIDATE CONCERNS PREVIOUSLY DISMISSED AS MISINFORMATION
Fauci served as chief medical advisor to President Donald Trump during the COVID-19 pandemic before later continuing in the role under President Joe Biden. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

A surprising recurring theme throughout the diaries is Fauci's growing awareness of his own public profile during the most intense months of the pandemic, which ultimately claimed more than 7 million officially reported lives worldwide, including roughly 1.2 million in the United States.
On April 7, 2020, after recording the latest pandemic developments, Fauci wrote: "Press still hot and heavy about me. Multiple stories per day directly or indirectly involving me."
SLACK MESSAGES RELEASED BY RAND PAUL APPEAR TO SHOW AUTHORS OF KEY COVID-19 ORIGIN PAPER HELD PRIVATE DOUBTS
Dr. Anthony Fauci, who led the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, became a central figure in the federal government's response to COVID-19. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

By May 21, after recording the latest pandemic figures — nearly 98,000 global deaths and more than 27,000 U.S. deaths — and documenting the day's White House coronavirus task force meetings, Fauci wrote that his "national and international fame is explosive and really unimaginable" and that it was "not hyperbole" to say he was "the most famous and talked about person in the country."

He added that Trump "seems to be enamored of me even though I am taking the spotlight away from him," writing that the two were developing "a very unique and interesting relationship." Fauci also noted that Secret Service agents had become so familiar with him they often waved him through White House security without checking his identification.

As the attention continued to grow, the diary increasingly documented how Fauci's prominence had expanded beyond public health. A month later, as the United States recorded what Fauci described as a record 40,000 new COVID-19 cases in a single day, he wrote that he had been invited to appear on "Dancing with the Stars."
LEGACY MEDIA IGNORES MASSIVE ANTHONY FAUCI DOCUMENT RELEASE ALLEGING HE MISLED CONGRESS ON COVID ORIGINS

Dr. Anthony Fauci emerged as a leading public face of the U.S. pandemic response, though his relationship with President Donald Trump grew increasingly strained as the pandemic wore on. (Jabin Botsford/The Washington Post/Getty Images)

The diaries also document Fauci's growing frustration with the Trump White House. On July 2, 2020, after warning that the country could be entering an "exponential" increase in COVID-19 cases heading into the Fourth of July weekend, Fauci wrote, "POTUS and his people have essentially dropped out and do not even recognize that an outbreak is ongoing."

He also complained that the White House was denying requests for him to appear on major television programs. Across multiple entries, Fauci criticized White House communications officials for restricting his television appearances, questioned the administration's public messaging and expressed frustration that media coverage increasingly portrayed him as being at odds with Trump.
ANTHONY FAUCI DELIVERED ONE OF THE WORST FIRST PITCHES IN BASEBALL HISTORY SIX YEARS AGO

Dr. Anthony Fauci throws out the ceremonial first pitch prior to the game between the New York Yankees and the Washington Nationals at Nationals Park on July 23, 2020, in Washington, D.C. (Getty Images)

Fauci also repeatedly defended himself against what he described as the "countless" profiles written about him. He wrote that White House officials were upset because the coverage made it appear he was becoming "a star that outshines" the president.

He also insisted several of the profiles had been written without interviewing him and wrote that he had "no desire to conflict with, embarrass or show up the POTUS," later deciding to stop participating in profile interviews altogether.

Taken together, the entries offer an unusually personal account of Fauci's role during one of the most consequential public health crises in modern U.S. history, capturing not only the government's internal deliberations but also his private concerns about the pandemic, his increasingly complicated relationship with the Trump White House and the extraordinary public attention that followed.

title: Trump's SAVE America Act stalls as McConnell's absence complicates Senate path
summary: Sen. Mitch McConnell's extended Senate absence complicates the SAVE America Act's path through budget reconciliation as Republicans scramble for votes.
story: President Donald Trump meets with GOP senators on Capitol Hill to lobby for the SAVE America Act, emphasizing the need for voter ID and other election integrity reforms. Fox News' Chad Pergram provides the latest on the push.

One key Republican’s extended absence and unclear timetable for return is slowing down several legislative priorities, and could impact President Donald Trump’s Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) America Act in an unexpected way.
And while sparse statements from Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and his office say he’s on the mend, there has yet to be a hard date for when he’ll come back to Congress.

It comes as Republicans are twisting and contorting Trump's top election priority into something that could pass the Senate. Though McConnell has voted against the bill before, he would be a key player in crafting what it would look like in the upper chamber.
TRUMP'S VOTER ID BILL CATCHES UNLIKELY BREAK AS MCCONNELL REMAINS SIDELINED
Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., has been away from the Senate for more than a month after a medical emergency. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"That could be an issue," Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., told Fox News Digital. "I think there are a lot of issues."

That’s because McConnell is chair of the Senate Rules Committee, which will likely be responsible for drafting the version of the SAVE America Act that could pass muster in budget reconciliation, the process that Trump is pushing the GOP to use to pass the bill.

The uncertainty around McConnell, coupled with the late Sen. Lindsey Graham’s recent death, throws a wrench into the process. Graham was chair of the Senate Budget Committee, and acted as quarterback through two dances with reconciliation over the past year.
SENATE RETURNS TO PACKED AGENDA AFTER GRAHAM'S DEATH SHRINKS GOP MARGIN

But Graham’s replacement on the panel, Johnson, could step in and draft language for SAVE America as chair of the Budget Committee — Graham leapfrogged Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chair Rand Paul, R-Ky., in 2025 to draft his portion of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

"That’s my understanding — it actually falls to budget," Johnson said. "So, again… this is still really early in the process, so I don't have all the answers by a long stretch. Plus, we've got to find out what the conference wants to do, and what Leader John Thune wants to do."

Senate Majority Leader Thune, R-S.D., is focusing on preventing a government shutdown, and is encouraging ongoing bipartisan negotiations on a funding deal to continue. And he has threatened to press pause on reconciliation by holding the House’s own budget framework until that objective is accomplished.
GOP RIFT GROWS AS THUNE HITS BRAKES ON TRUMP'S ELECTION BILL TO AVERT SHUTDOWN

One key Republican’s extended absence and unclear timetable for return is slowing down several legislative priorities, and could impact President Donald Trump’s SAVE America Act in an unexpected way. (Mark Schiefelbein/The Associated Press )
He reiterated to Fox News Digital that Republicans don’t have the votes to pass the SAVE America Act, and may not have the votes to pass a budget resolution in the upper chamber.
And he noted that the SAVE America Act would have to comply with the Senate’s strict rules for reconciliation that unlock the 50-vote threshold, which the current version of the bill does not.

Getting the legislation to a point where it wouldn’t slam into those guardrails has remained an open and difficult question for Republicans — Thune suggested that it could work if it's "very carefully structured based upon incentive, mostly grant money," for states.

"So, you know, we're gonna do everything we can to move that forward," Thune said. "But as I told you before, the math on that hasn't changed yet. It's still likely to be a 60-vote exercise, even if it's done with a budget resolution."

Trump demanded Republicans ram through their own budget resolution before they leave Washington, D.C., until after Labor Day on Truth Social Friday to fund defense, agriculture and pass "as much of the SAVE AMERICA ACT as possible."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Our voters will be extremely happy — And even impressed," Trump said.
Meanwhile, Thune has received criticism from Republicans for his plan to hold up the reconciliation process in favor of averting a shutdown.

Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., told Fox News Digital the only option to pass SAVE America was through reconciliation, and he’s been working on his own plan in the background, and believes it could survive the Senate’s "Byrd" test.

"I can't guarantee it, but it's a — I consider it to be a credible argument," Kennedy said. "And I will try to do that, and I will try to, at the right time, bring my colleagues, and, more importantly, the parliamentarian, along. But if we don't do it through reconciliation, through the House reconciliation, we won't get it done."
"And I’m not sure it will work, but I think it might," he continued. "It’s at least a 50/50 shot."
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: EXCLUSIVE: Legal group tells NYPD cops they can contact ICE directly despite blue city's sanctuary rules
summary: America First Legal's guide tells NYPD officers they can contact ICE directly despite New York City sanctuary city policies under Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
story: Border czar Tom Homan criticizes NYC Mayor Mamdani, a Democratic socialist, for his 'pride' in New York being a sanctuary city. Homan argues that these policies prevent cooperation with federal immigration enforcement, potentially leading to tragic consequences, exemplified by the Laken Riley case. He emphasizes the importance of law and order.

EXCLUSIVE: A conservative legal group is telling New York City police officers they can contact U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) directly, even if local sanctuary policies say otherwise, releasing a new guide as border czar Tom Homan prepares a major immigration enforcement surge in the nation's largest city.

Fox News Digital has obtained an unreleased 35-page handbook titled "Law Enforcement Officer Immigration Cooperation Guide" from America First Legal (AFL) that tells state and local police officers they can share a person's immigration-status information directly with ICE even if New York City or other sanctuary city policies say otherwise.

The guide argues that Section 1373 of federal law bars state and local governments from preventing officers from sharing citizenship or immigration-status information with federal immigration authorities like ICE.
TOM HOMAN WARNS ICE SURGE COMING TO NEW YORK CITY AS MAMDANI BOASTS ABOUT SANCTUARY STATUS
White House border czar Tom Homan attends a news conference along the southern border. (Mike Blake/Reuters, File)
America First Legal is a nonprofit which describes itself as "founded to unapologetically and boldly defend the rights of everyday Americans."

The guide arrives days after Homan revealed he had reviewed plans to deploy "more ICE agents than you've ever seen" into New York City after Mayor Zohran Mamdani signed an executive order reinforcing the city's sanctuary-status policies.

The guide repeatedly cites Section 1373 of federal immigration law, arguing that state and local governments "may not prohibit, or in any way restrict" officials from sending immigration-status information to federal authorities.
DOJ ESCALATES BLUE-STATE ICE STANDOFF AFTER STATES REFUSE KEY FEDERAL REQUEST

Federal agents patrol the halls of immigration court at the Jacob K. Javitz Federal Building. According to White House border czar Tom Homan, ICE will increase its operations in New York City due to its status as a sanctuary city. (Getty Images, File)

It tells officers they may contact ICE's 24-hour Law Enforcement Support Center to verify a person's immigration status using only a name and date of birth and says officers may do so "regardless of any local directive telling you not to," according to the document obtained by Fox News Digital.
The release comes as the Trump administration prepares to dramatically increase immigration enforcement in New York.
Homan told Fox News last week that a significant ICE operation is coming to the city after self-described democratic socialist Mamdani reaffirmed New York's sanctuary policies.
NYC MAYOR ZOHRAN MAMDANI RELEASES AUDIT ACCUSING FEDERAL IMMIGRATION AGENTS OF MISLEADING TACTICS
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the Trump administration continue to clash over immigration enforcement. (Lev Radin/Pacific Press/LightRocket via Getty Images, File)
"It's coming," Homan said. "There's going to be a surge, and there needs to be a surge."
While Homan declined to discuss operational details, he said ICE would not back away from enforcing immigration law despite opposition from city leaders.
The guide comes as Mamdani and the Trump administration continue to clash over immigration enforcement.
Mamdani's Executive Order 13 directs the NYPD to review, update and train officers on department policies governing communication, cooperation and coordination with federal immigration authorities.

The order says the city believes "the aggressive tactics that certain non-local law enforcement agencies use in pursuing civil immigration enforcement actions... hinder public safety by creating a culture of fear."

America First Legal argues those local rules cannot lawfully prevent an officer from voluntarily sharing immigration-status information with ICE because federal law supersedes conflicting local policies.

The guide also argues sanctuary policies could create legal risks for the officials who enforce them. AFL contends some officials could face federal criminal charges for obstructing immigration enforcement and that victims of crimes allegedly committed by illegal immigrants released despite ICE detainers could, in some cases, sue those officials under federal civil RICO law.
The organization is also inviting officers who believe they were threatened, disciplined or retaliated against for cooperating with ICE to seek confidential legal representation.

"Politicians who hide behind sanctuary policies are not above the law, and they have no right to bully or gag the officers who are trying to keep their communities safe," AFL senior counsel James Rogers said in a statement accompanying the guide.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Gene Hamilton, president of America First Legal, said officers "should never be forced to choose between following federal law and following unlawful directives to appease politicians committed to sanctuary policies."
New York City Hall did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
Fox News Digital's Taylor Penley contributed to this reporting.
Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

title: Your home is empty. Do burglars already know?
summary: Burglary crews linked to Patrick Mahomes and Travis Kelce break-ins used public schedules and data brokers to target homes while owners traveled.
story: Retired LAPD lieutenant Jeff Wenninger explains how criminals exploit obituaries, routines and public clues to time home break-ins and what families can do to reduce risk.
In Argentina, authorities recently arrested three Chilean men wanted in the U.S. in connection with a South American theft group accused of burglarizing the homes of professional athletes.

Federal prosecutors linked the group to break-ins involving Kansas City Chiefs stars Patrick Mahomes and Travis Kelce, Milwaukee Bucks player Bobby Portis and other athletes. Two of the suspects were also arrested in connection with a burglary at the home of tennis legend Juan Martín del Potro in Argentina.

According to prosecutors, the group identified targets through publicly available schedules and location information, then struck while athletes were away or playing games. Separately, the FBI has warned that international theft groups surveil homeowners to learn their routines and advises travelers to avoid announcing vacations on social media.

Online criminals can research your address, family, travel plans and estimated property value without ever driving down your street. Here's how criminals piece together those digital clues and what you can do to make your home harder to target.
ALLEGED BURGLARY CREW THAT TARGETED PATRICK MAHOMES AND TRAVIS KELCE HOMES ARRESTED IN ARGENTINA: REPORT

Alleged members of a South American theft ring pose with stolen valuables. Federal investigators say the group targeted professional athletes while they were away competing in games. (U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida/Photo by Bryan M. Bennett/Getty Images)
CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?," has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
How online criminals target empty homes

It may be tempting to assume these crimes only affect people with mansions, expensive cars and celebrity lifestyles. Those cases make the news, but professional athletes and entertainers are far from the only targets. Security researchers and law enforcement agencies have tracked burglary crews using the same methods against everyday homeowners.

One recent case involved a Los Angeles content creator whose Silver Lake home was burglarized while she was traveling. Thieves reportedly took tens of thousands of dollars in designer goods. She had shared that she was away, which gave anyone watching her public account a useful clue.

For retirees, the risk can grow as travel becomes more frequent. You may finally take the cruise you have planned for years, spend a month in Florida each winter or take a road trip to visit your grandchildren. Those trips also create more opportunities to post "we made it" from an airport, beach or campground while your home sits empty.
How family members can expose your travel plans

Maybe you wait until you return home before posting vacation photos. However, someone in your life may share the information for you. A spouse might tag the airport. An adult child could post a picture of the grandchildren in front of your house. A neighbor might mention that you are away on your annual trip.

You have limited control over what other people share, so talk with your family before traveling. Ask everyone to wait until you return before posting locations, travel photos or details about how long you will be gone. Watching what your family posts helps, but social media provides only part of the information criminals can collect.
How property records help criminals research your home

Investigators in Riverside, California, say they routinely find Zillow and Redfin searches on the phones of arrested burglary suspects. These sites may reveal an estimated property value, past sale prices and photos from an old listing. In some cases, criminals can view interior layouts, doors, windows and rooms before they approach the property.

Public property records can also reveal the owner's name, mailing address and purchase history. Meanwhile, data broker and people-search sites may connect that address with phone numbers, relatives, previous homes and other personal details. Combine "this person is traveling" with "this home has significant value," and criminals have the beginnings of a target list.
AI VOICE SCAMS CAN CLONE YOUR FAMILY’S VOICE
Burglars can use social media posts, public records and real estate listings to determine when a home may be empty. (PC Photography / Getty Images)
What strangers can find about your home online

Search your name, phone number and home address to see what appears. You may find people-search profiles that list your age, relatives, address history and possible phone numbers. Real estate websites may still display old interior photos, even when you purchased the home years ago. Someone could use those details to connect your social media account with a specific property.

Want to see what information data brokers may have about you? Run a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web: Cyberguy.com. You should receive the results within an hour.
8 ways to protect your home before your next trip

These steps can reduce the amount of useful information available to someone researching your home. They work best alongside basic home security measures, such as an alarm system, a doorbell camera, light timers and secure storage for valuables.
Save airport, hotel and sightseeing photos until you are back home. Real-time posts can tell strangers where you are and confirm that your house may be empty.
Tell your spouse, children, grandchildren and travel companions to wait before sharing your location or mentioning your travel dates.
Limit posts to people you know. Remove followers you do not recognize and check whether old public posts reveal your routines, vehicles or home address.
Ask a trusted neighbor to collect mail, newspapers and deliveries. You can also place a temporary hold on your mail before an extended trip.
Use timers or smart plugs to turn lights on and off at different times. Leaving every light off for two weeks can make an empty home easier to spot.
WHAT A SCAMMER SEES THE MOMENT THEY GOOGLE YOUR NAME
Surveillance footage shows a 2024 looting carried out by a Chilean crime ring at a Michigan home, shared with Fox 2 Detroit by a homeowner. (WJBK)
Search your address on Zillow, Redfin and other real estate sites to see whether old listings reveal interior rooms, entrances or the layout of your home.

On Redfin, use a desktop browser and sign in. Select your name in the upper-right corner, choose My homes, select your claimed property and click Edit Photos. Check Hide listing photos, then select Yes, Hide Photos. This feature applies to off-market homes and currently does not appear in the Redfin mobile app.

On Zillow, sign in and select your profile icon, followed by Your Home. Choose your property and claim ownership if you have not already done so. From the Owner View, select Edit Facts. You can remove individual photos, delete all photos or check the option to hide photos from public view. Select Save Changes when finished.

Some off-market homes may not offer the editing option. In that case, submit a request to Zillow Customer Support. Other real estate sites may require you to claim the property, contact customer support or ask the original listing agent for help.
Data broker and people-search sites can connect your name, phone number, relatives and home address. Search for your information and request removal from sites that display it.

A data removal service can automate requests across hundreds of covered brokers and continue checking whether your information returns. It cannot erase government property records or every old real estate listing, so use it alongside the other home protection steps above.
You can also submit removal requests yourself, though the process may take more time and require repeat checks.
Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting Cyberguy.com.
Search your name, address and phone number every few months. Look for new people-search profiles, outdated listings and social media posts that reveal more than you intended.
Kurt's key takeaways

Burglary crews no longer need to spend days watching your street. Social media can reveal when you are away, while property records, real estate listings and people-search sites can reveal where you live and what your home may be worth. Retirement often brings more time for travel, which creates more opportunities for you or a family member to announce that your home is empty. You have limited control over public records and what your relatives post. However, you can delay travel posts, tighten privacy settings, remove old listing photos and reduce your exposure on data broker sites. Removing your personal information will never make you invisible. It can still make your home harder for online criminals to research and target.

title: What to look for in antivirus software without the jargon
summary: A simple antivirus checklist covers real-time protection, malware and ransomware defense, firewall tools and scam detection without technical jargon.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Shopping for antivirus software can feel harder than it should. Many product pages lead with buzzwords, lab scores and long feature lists. Most of us just want a simple answer: Will this help keep my computer safe without making life harder?

That question gets more important every day. Scammers use fake texts, phishing emails, bogus websites and infected downloads to trick you into giving up your money, passwords or access to your personal files.

The good news? You do not need to understand every technical term to make a smart choice. A strong antivirus program should automatically monitor for threats, help block malware and ransomware, include firewall protection and run quietly in the background.

HALLUSQUATTING AI ATTACK COULD HIJACK YOUR COMPUTER
Real-time antivirus protection helps watch for threats while you browse, open attachments, download files or click links. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Real-time antivirus protection should work automatically

The first thing to look for is real-time protection. That means the software keeps watching while you browse, open attachments, download files or click links. Threats can show up at any moment. Malware can hide inside downloads, fake websites or links that look harmless. If your antivirus only works when you remember to run a scan, you may miss the moment when protection counts most. When comparing options, ask one simple question: Does this protect me automatically? For most people, automatic protection is the safer choice because it works before you remember to check.
Antivirus software should help block malware and ransomware

Many people still use the word virus for almost every online threat. Today's risks go much wider. Strong antivirus software should help protect against malware, spyware, ransomware and suspicious activity. Ransomware deserves special attention because it can lock your personal files, photos and documents. Once that happens, getting access back can become stressful, expensive or impossible. So, instead of getting stuck on product jargon, look for clear language about the threats the software helps stop. You want protection that covers the problems people actually face today.
REDHOOK ANDROID MALWARE CAN QUIETLY HIJACK YOUR PHONE
A strong antivirus tool should help block malware, ransomware, spyware and suspicious activity before they reach your files. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Firewall protection adds another layer of security

The word firewall sounds technical, but the idea is simple. A firewall helps monitor traffic going in and out of your device. It can also help block suspicious connections. That matters because some threats try to communicate with your device or send data out without your knowledge. A firewall gives your system another layer of defense. When shopping, check whether firewall protection is included. Some antivirus products offer stronger firewall tools than others, so this can be a meaningful difference.
Strong antivirus software should run quietly

Many people avoid antivirus software because they worry it will slow down their computer. That concern makes sense. Security software that constantly interrupts you can get ignored, delayed or turned off. Performance should matter. Good antivirus software should run in the background without making everyday tasks feel harder. You should still be able to browse, work, stream and manage files without constant pop-ups or delays. For most mainstream users, the best choice often comes down to everyday comfort. If the software feels easy to live with, you are more likely to keep it running.
Frequent antivirus updates help fight new threats

Online threats keep changing. Scammers adjust their tactics. Malware changes. Fake websites appear quickly, then disappear and show up somewhere else. That is why updates matter. Antivirus software works best when the provider keeps improving detection as threats evolve. Before choosing a product, look for signs that it receives regular updates. You want protection that keeps pace with newer risks rather than software that feels frozen in time.
Scam protection belongs on your antivirus checklist

Many attacks begin before malware ever reaches your device. A fake delivery notice, phishing email or bogus text can push you to click a bad link or enter personal information on a fake site. That makes scam protection worth checking. Good security software should help flag suspicious links, fake messages and risky websites before they create a bigger problem. AI-powered scam detection can provide another layer of help by analyzing questionable content and warning you when something appears unsafe. This can be especially useful during everyday browsing, shopping and email use.
Scam protection can help flag fake emails, risky links and suspicious websites before one wrong click becomes a bigger problem. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What this antivirus checklist means for you

You do not need to compare every technical feature on every product page. Start with the basics. Look for real-time protection that runs automatically. Make sure the software helps block malware and ransomware. Check for firewall protection. Pay attention to performance. Also, look for regular updates and scam detection. That approach helps you focus on what actually affects your daily life. The goal is simple: protect your device without turning computer security into a second job.
How to choose the right antivirus software
Use this checklist to narrow down your options. Look for real-time protection against viruses, malware, spyware and ransomware, along with a firewall that helps block suspicious connections.

Usability matters too. Security software should run quietly in the background without slowing down your device or interrupting you with constant alerts. Before choosing a plan, compare its features, device limits, introductory price and renewal cost.
The most useful question remains practical: Will this protect you automatically, cover the threats you may encounter and stay easy to use every day?
Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.
Kurt's key takeaways

Antivirus software can feel confusing because companies often make it sound more complicated than necessary. Most people are not shopping for technical jargon. They want protection that works before a bad click turns into a costly problem. The best approach is to look past the marketing language and focus on what the software actually does for you. Real-time protection, ransomware defense, firewall tools, scam detection and regular updates all matter. Performance matters too. If security software slows down your device or interrupts you constantly, you may stop using it. Look for an option that runs quietly in the background and remains easy to manage. The key is choosing antivirus software you will keep turned on, keep updated and trust when something suspicious appears.

title: AI wearable watches you to predict what you need
summary: The iKairos AI wearable features an inward-facing camera and voice detection to anticipate your needs, raising significant privacy questions.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel explains ACTXA's Core Smart Ring, an AI-powered wearable offering non-invasive glucose monitoring. This new technology senses blood flow and pulse, using machine learning to detect elevated blood sugar. Siegel notes its importance given the nearly quadrupled global diabetes cases since 2000, emphasizing lifestyle changes alongside technological advancements for better care.

Would you wear a small AI device that periodically looks at you and studies the world around you? A Singapore-based smart hardware and AI company, Lingverse, is betting people may be ready for that level of attention. Lingverse has raised $29 million to develop an AI wearable called iKairos. The company describes it as a personal AI guardian that can offer help before you ask.

The device can turn toward your surroundings or toward you. Lingverse says this two-way view could give its AI more context about what is happening in your life. That extra perspective could make AI more useful in daily life. However, it also creates a very personal trade-off. The device may need to observe you closely before it can understand what you need.
COULD A PAINT-ON ELECTRONIC TATTOO SPOT HEART ATTACKS?
The iKairos AI wearable can observe its user and surrounding environment, raising questions about convenience, consent and privacy. (Lingverse)
CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?", has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.

Why an AI wearable wants to watch you

Most AI assistants wait for a command. You ask a question or tap a button, then the software responds. Wearable AI devices can gather more context because they travel with you. Many use outward-facing cameras to identify objects or describe what appears nearby.

Lingverse wants iKairos to gather a second type of context. The device can turn its camera toward the person wearing it. Lingverse says this dual-perspective design could help iKairos understand both you and your environment. In turn, the device may be able to choose a more useful moment to offer assistance.
How iKairos tries to predict your needs

Lingverse calls iKairos a proactive AI device. Instead of waiting for every prompt, it could use context to decide when to step in. For example, a context-aware assistant might know you have an appointment and notice that you remain at home as the departure time approaches. It could then remind you to leave. Lingverse has not confirmed that this exact feature will be available at launch.

Lingverse says iKairos will learn about you over time. That memory could help it choose when to offer a question, reminder or suggestion. When we asked what specific tasks or predictions iKairos will handle at launch, Lingverse described its broader goal of anticipating your needs and adapting to your routine. The company did not provide concrete launch examples.
AI CHATBOTS TAKE HEAT OVER LEFT-WING BIAS: ‘NO LONGER BE CONSIDERED NEUTRAL’
Lingverse says the iKairos wearable device analyzes occasional still images, detects human voices and deletes raw photos after processing them. (Lingverse)
How the iKairos AI wearable works

Lingverse describes iKairos as a modular device. You can wear it or place it on a desk. The device can shift its gaze between you and the surrounding area. This allows it to collect context from either direction.

Lingverse says iKairos captures no video. Instead, its camera takes occasional still photos. The company says each image is discarded immediately after the AI analyzes it, leaving no browsable library of raw images on the device or in the cloud. The device picks up audio only after detecting a human voice, according to Lingverse. The company says it will not continuously record everything around you. However, Lingverse has yet to explain how long voice-triggered audio remains available during or after analysis.

The device captures information locally, but its AI analysis happens in the cloud. Lingverse says no information leaves the device without your explicit consent. Lingverse is targeting 12 to 16 hours of battery life. The company says actual runtime will vary based on how often the device captures information, how frequently it syncs and the environment where you use it.
AI wearable privacy protections and concerns

An inward-facing camera will likely make privacy the biggest issue surrounding iKairos. Lingverse says the hardware includes a physical camera shutter. Closing it blocks the camera and gives you a visible privacy control.

You will also be able to press and hold a control to place iKairos in silent mode. Lingverse says this stops the device from listening, while the screen and an indicator light confirm that silent mode is active.

According to Lingverse, you decide what gets uploaded for cloud analysis. The company says it encrypts information while it travels, while it remains stored in the cloud and while it stays locally on the device.

Lingverse also says you can choose how long it keeps your data. You can permanently delete an individual item or close your account, which the company says clears all content connected to it from the cloud.
How a former home robot inspired the new wearable

The idea behind iKairos grew from an earlier home robot called Jibo. Jibo was a small tabletop robot with an expressive screen for a face. It gained attention after a 2014 crowdfunding campaign and later appeared on TIME's Best Inventions list.

Its expressive face and animated movements helped set it apart from conventional smart speakers. Yet the robot stayed in one place, which limited its usefulness. The company behind Jibo eventually closed. In 2019, the robot delivered an emotional farewell message to its owners before its services wound down.

Lingverse founder and CEO Jiawei Gu previously served on Jibo's board. According to Lingverse, he also worked on human-computer interaction at Microsoft Research and Baidu. Gu later developed the Luka Reading Robot. Lingverse says that the reading companion has sold roughly 10 million units. Now, Gu wants to continue Jibo's social robot concept with current AI technology. iKairos keeps the expressive face while adding mobility and a deeper understanding of you.
AI BUILDS VIRTUAL HOMES WHERE ROBOTS LEARN FROM THEIR MISTAKES
Lingverse’s iKairos wearable uses an inward-facing camera and cloud-based artificial intelligence to anticipate when users may need help. (Lingverse)
AI wearable price, subscription and release details
Lingverse says iKairos preorders will begin during the third quarter of 2026 at ikairos.world. Each device will ship within 90 days of the preorder, according to the company.

Exact pricing will be released closer to launch. Lingverse says core features will work through a free tier, while more advanced capabilities will require a subscription. The company has yet to reveal which features require payment or how much the subscription will cost.
Kurt's key takeaways

iKairos gives us an early look at where wearable AI could be headed. The idea has promise, especially if it can step in with useful help without recording your entire day. Lingverse has now filled in some of the privacy blanks around still images, voice detection and data controls. Still, the AI analysis happens in the cloud, so you will want to know exactly when information leaves the device and what you are agreeing to share. The targeted 12 to 16 hours of battery life could get you through most of the day. The bigger question is what iKairos will actually do for you when it launches. We also need the final price and subscription details before we know whether the trade-off is worth it.

Would you wear an AI companion that uses occasional photos and voice detection to understand your day, or would any inward-facing camera feel like one camera too many? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com.

title: Self-dressing clothes could help older adults
summary: KAIST and Stanford researchers built soft robotic tubes into fabric that use air pressure to guide clothing into place in about 10 seconds flat.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Most of us get dressed every day without thinking twice about it. However, a stiff shoulder can make pulling on a shirt surprisingly difficult, while balance problems can turn a simple pair of pants into a real challenge. That is what makes a new invention from South Korea's KAIST and Stanford University worth watching.

Researchers have created self-dressing clothes with soft, air-powered robots built into the fabric. Once activated, the garment moves along the body and helps guide itself into place, even while the wearer moves. The technology remains an early research project, but it shows how future clothing could help older adults get dressed with less assistance and stay independent at home longer.
CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?" , has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
NEW YORK SCHOOL DISTRICT TO DEPLOY HUMANOID ROBOT IN CLASSROOMS THIS FALL
The self-dressing system uses soft, air-powered robots to guide sleeves, a jacket and pants into place around the body. (KAIST)
How self-dressing clothes could support independence

Getting dressed ranks among the basic activities that often determine whether someone can live independently. When mobility or dexterity declines, people may need a spouse, family member or professional caregiver to help with a deeply personal routine.

The researchers behind the project say dressing challenges can reduce autonomy and increase reliance on caregivers. They designed the system for people with limited mobility, including older adults and those recovering from injuries. Stanford researchers have also identified dressing assistance as an important use for future home robots. The university says assistive technology could help older adults remain in their homes as caregiving needs increase.
Why dressing can become physically difficult

Dressing requires more movement than many people realize. You need to reach behind your body, lift your arms and shift your weight while handling fabric. Arthritis may make gripping or pulling clothing painful. Meanwhile, shoulder problems can limit your reach. Recovery from hip or knee surgery can also make bending difficult.

Balance adds another concern. Pulling on pants often requires someone to stand briefly on one leg or bend toward the floor. For a person who already feels unsteady, that familiar routine can become stressful. Self-dressing clothes could eventually reduce some of that reaching and pulling. However, researchers still need clinical studies to learn how well the system works for people with real mobility limitations.
How KAIST and Stanford's robotic clothing works

The researchers call their system SWAG, which stands for Self-Wearing Adaptive Garment. Instead of placing a large robotic arm next to the person, the team built flexible robotic tubes into the clothing. Air pressure causes these soft structures to unfold and grow along the body.

The movement turns the garment inside out as it advances. That approach allows the clothing to follow the person's shape while reducing friction between the fabric and skin. Think of ivy growing around a wall or tree. The plant advances from its tip rather than dragging its entire length forward. The soft robot uses a similar motion, which helps it follow curves and move across different surfaces.
In this demonstration, the robotic garment unfurls over the legs while the wearer remains seated. (KAIST)
A rainy bike ride sparked the robotic clothing idea
The idea began when KAIST postdoctoral researcher Nam Gyun Kim was riding his bike when it began to rain. As he kept moving, he wondered how helpful it would be if a raincoat could put itself on.

That simple idea led to a much bigger thought. Instead of making your body do all the pulling, reaching and twisting, what if the clothing could move into place on its own? From there, Kim and the research team began developing garments that use soft robotics to help dress the person wearing them.
How fast self-dressing clothes can work

Kim says putting on a full suit takes about 10 seconds. The published paper provides additional timing from individual demonstrations. A jacket moved into place in about 13 seconds, while the pants demonstration took roughly 21 seconds. A sleeve prototype took about 14 seconds.

The researchers tested sleeves, jackets and pants. Their results showed that the garments could unfold along the body while keeping contact forces within the team's safety limits. The system also relies on its physical design instead of a complicated control program. That could eventually help simplify the hardware needed for dressing assistance.
Why soft robotic clothing could feel more natural

Many existing dressing robots use rigid mechanical arms. Those systems must handle loose fabric while carefully avoiding uncomfortable contact with the person. They may also require the person to hold a fixed pose while the robot completes the task. That setup could feel awkward inside a bedroom or bathroom.

The KAIST and Stanford design takes a different approach by placing the robotic mechanism inside the garment. The clothing becomes the helper. Because the system uses soft materials, it can bend around the body rather than approaching it with a hard mechanical structure. KAIST says this design reduces physical strain and supports safer contact.
COULD A PAINT-ON ELECTRONIC TATTOO SPOT HEART ATTACKS?
Flexible robotic tubes built into the jacket help pull the sleeves and fabric into position with less effort from the wearer. (KAIST)
Where self-dressing clothes could be used first

Older adults and people with disabilities represent a major potential use for the technology. KAIST also sees possibilities for rehabilitation patients who need temporary assistance after an injury or medical procedure. However, industrial workplaces may adopt the idea sooner.

Semiconductor employees frequently put on protective cleanroom clothing. Emergency workers may also need to suit up quickly while carrying other equipment. The researchers believe air-powered garments could help people put on protective clothing without relying heavily on their hands. The published study also discusses possible medical uses, such as helping healthcare workers apply protective coverings or compression bandages. Those applications remain potential future directions.
What self-dressing clothes still need to prove

The current system remains a research prototype connected to a pneumatic base station. Researchers have yet to announce a consumer price or release date. Several everyday questions remain unanswered. The garments would need to fit different body shapes and movement patterns. Designers would also need to address washing, storage and portable air power.

The research team says future versions may use adjustable sheaths or elastic materials to fit a wider range of bodies. The researchers also want to automate the garment-loading process and improve the controls.

Most importantly, the team says clinical trials involving people with mobility impairments will be essential. Those tests could show whether the clothing feels comfortable and works reliably outside the lab. Researchers also need to explore how the garment comes off. The current work concentrates mainly on dressing, while automated removal remains a future possibility.
What this means to you

You probably will not find robotic clothing hanging in a local store anytime soon. Yet this research gives us a useful preview of where assistive technology may be heading. For you or someone you care about, the biggest benefit could be control over a private daily routine. Clothing that handles part of the pulling and positioning could make mornings less tiring.
It could also delay the point when someone needs another person present simply to get dressed. That possibility still depends on testing, affordability and a design people feel comfortable wearing.
Kurt's key takeaways

Self-dressing clothes may sound unusual, but the need behind them is easy to understand. Arthritis, limited mobility or recovery from surgery can make getting dressed frustrating and exhausting. For older adults, a garment that helps guide itself into place could mean more privacy, less reliance on a caregiver and more confidence starting the day. The KAIST and Stanford system still has a long way to go. Researchers need to make it portable, test it with people who have mobility challenges and prove it can work safely in a home. Even so, the idea shows how technology could support independence through something as familiar as the clothes you already wear.

title: ClickLock Mac malware locks apps until you give in
summary: ClickLock Mac malware uses a fake verification page to trick users into pasting a Terminal command, then steals passwords and cryptocurrency wallets.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A routine "verify you are human" page should never ask you to open Terminal, the Mac app used to run computer commands. Yet that is how a new malware attack appears to get onto a Mac. The page tells you to copy and paste a command into Terminal. It then shows a convincing progress bar while the command quietly downloads malicious software in the background.

Next, a password box may appear that looks like a normal macOS request. If you cancel it, the malware can come back after you sign in again and repeatedly close Finder, your browser and other apps. Your Mac may feel almost impossible to use until you enter your login password.

The malware, called ClickLock, is built to steal personal information from your Mac. It searches for saved passwords, browser data and cryptocurrency wallet files. It can also install a hidden tool that lets an attacker reconnect to your computer later and control it remotely.

Researchers at cybersecurity company Group-IB discovered the malicious script on VirusTotal, an online service that checks files for threats. Someone first uploaded it there on June 9, 2026, yet none of the security tools on the platform detected it at the time of the researchers' report. Group-IB says the campaign has targeted at least 100 systems across 33 countries since May.
Here is how ClickLock takes over a Mac and what you can do to protect yourself.
CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?" , has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
FAKE PASSWORD-MANAGER ALERTS COULD PUT YOUR VAULT AT RISK
ClickLock may begin with a fake verification page that tells you to paste a command into Terminal. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What is ClickLock Mac malware?

ClickLock is a set of malicious scripts designed to steal sensitive information from a Mac. The malware can collect your Mac login password and browser data. It also searches for cryptocurrency wallet files, password manager extensions and information stored in macOS Keychain.
One component installs a persistent backdoor. That hidden connection can allow an attacker to access your Mac remotely even after the other parts of ClickLock remove themselves.
ClickLock gets started without exploiting a known macOS flaw. It also does not need admin-level access at the beginning. Instead, the attack depends on convincing you to run the command yourself.
How a fake verification starts the attack

Group-IB believes ClickLock likely spreads through a tactic called ClickFix. ClickFix attacks show you a fake error or verification request. The page then gives you a command that supposedly fixes the problem.

In this case, the ClickLock script displays a fake Cloudflare verification sequence after you paste the command into Terminal. An animated progress bar cycles through reassuring messages about checking browser signals and confirming you are human.

Meanwhile, the script disables keyboard interruptions and hides the Terminal cursor. It then downloads several malicious components in the background. Researchers have yet to confirm the exact landing pages used in the campaign. They also do not know whether people reached them through malicious search results, compromised websites, phishing messages or social media. However, the script's design strongly points to a ClickFix-style lure.
The password trap starts with a convincing pop-up

After the malware begins running, it displays a fake macOS password window. The pop-up uses your real username and an Apple icon downloaded by the attacker. If you enter a password, ClickLock checks it against your Mac. When the password works, the malware records it and sends it to the attacker through Telegram.

An incorrect password brings up another request. If you cancel the window, ClickLock installs two LaunchAgents. A LaunchAgent is a macOS instruction that can automatically run software when you sign in. In this case, the LaunchAgents bring the password-stealing components back at your next login.
HALLUSQUATTING AI ATTACK COULD HIJACK YOUR COMPUTER
The malware can repeatedly close apps and pressure you to enter your Mac login password. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
ClickLock can make your Mac feel unusable

When the password-stealing module returns, it begins closing visible apps every 210 milliseconds. It targets Finder, the Dock and Terminal. It also shuts down Activity Monitor, System Settings, Spotlight and common web browsers.

The fake password window may remain as the only useful item on your screen. That can make your Mac look broken while pressuring you to enter your password. Group-IB found that the loop can run for about 83 hours. It stops earlier when the malware captures a valid password.
A real Keychain prompt makes the attack more convincing

A second ClickLock component targets Chrome's Safe Storage key. Chromium-based browsers use this key to help encrypt passwords, cookies and autofill information stored on your Mac. An attacker with the key and copied browser databases may be able to decrypt that information offline.

This part of the attack triggers a genuine macOS Keychain authorization prompt. However, the malware caused the request. ClickLock then runs another process-closing loop while waiting for you to approve access. Researchers found that this loop repeats every 200 milliseconds and can continue for nearly 35 days. The script also suppresses macOS NotificationCenter for roughly six hours. That could hide warnings or notifications that might reveal the attack.
What ClickLock can steal from your Mac
ClickLock searches for information across eight browsers. Those browsers include Chrome, Firefox, Brave, Microsoft Edge, Opera, Vivaldi, Arc and Chromium.
The targeted browser information includes:
Saved usernames and passwordsCookies and active session dataAutofill informationBookmarks and browser storageCryptocurrency wallet extensionsPassword manager extension data
Saved usernames and passwords
Cookies and active session data
Autofill information
Bookmarks and browser storage
Cryptocurrency wallet extensions
Password manager extension data

The malware also searches for desktop cryptocurrency wallets and encrypted wallet vaults. It can collect cached blockchain addresses across several networks. Other targets include macOS Keychain, Terminal command histories and FileZilla server details. The malware also records basic information about your Mac and its public IP address. ClickLock packages the collected information into a ZIP archive. It uploads that archive through Telegram's Bot API. Files larger than 40 MB get divided into smaller pieces, while retry code keeps trying after network failures.
If your Mac starts acting this way, shut it down and restart in Safe Mode before entering any password. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
ClickLock can leave a backdoor behind

One ClickLock component uses a modified version of the open-source GSocket tool. The malware installs a reverse shell, which gives the attacker a command-line connection to your Mac. On macOS, it disguises the backdoor as an iCloud-related process.

ClickLock uses a LaunchAgent and scheduled commands to keep the backdoor running. It also changes shell configuration files. Most of the other ClickLock modules delete themselves after completing their work. The GSocket component remains installed, which means the attacker may retain access after your Mac appears to return to normal.
Why ClickLock may be difficult to detect

The original ClickLock script had zero detections on VirusTotal when Group-IB analyzed it. Security vendors may update their detection tools as they learn more about the threat. The attackers also stored payloads on compromised websites that previously had clean reputations. Some components run without saving a normal file to the drive. Others erase themselves after stealing data.

However, ClickLock still produces suspicious activity while it runs. Warning signs include nonstop app closures, repeated password requests and sudden access to multiple browser folders. Security tools may also detect unusual connections to Telegram's API. For you, the earliest warning sign is much simpler. A website tells you to paste a command into Terminal. Legitimate human verification happens inside your browser. It should never require you to run a Terminal command.
Ways to stay safe from ClickLock Mac malware
These steps can help you avoid the ClickLock trap and respond quickly if the password loop starts.

Leave the page when it tells you to open Terminal and paste a command. A polished design offers no proof that the request is safe. Familiar logos can also be copied. Group-IB warns that a website asking you to use Terminal for verification is attempting to compromise your system.
Terminal commands can download software and change important settings. Never run an unfamiliar command simply to see what happens. Ask a trusted technical professional to inspect it first.

Think about what you were doing when the password window appeared. A website verification should have no reason to ask for your Mac login password. It should also have no reason to request access to Chrome information stored in Keychain. Cancel the request when the timing feels wrong.

Install macOS updates and keep automatic security updates turned on. Apple builds malware protection into macOS through Gatekeeper, Notarization and XProtect. Apple updates XProtect automatically as it identifies new malware. However, no built-in protection can eliminate every risk when you manually run a malicious command.

Strong antivirus software can provide another layer of protection against malicious files and suspicious behavior. Still, a clean scan cannot guarantee that ClickLock left nothing behind. The backdoor persists after other components erase themselves. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com

Do not enter your password to make the pop-up disappear. Press and hold your Mac's power button for up to 10 seconds until the computer shuts down. On a MacBook with Touch ID, press and hold the Touch ID button. Group-IB recommends forcing a shutdown when your Mac becomes unresponsive and keeps requesting your password. The company then recommends starting the Mac in Safe Mode.

Mac with Apple silicon: Wait until the Mac shuts down completely. Press and hold the power button until "Loading startup options" appears. Select your startup volume. Hold the Shift key, then click Continue in Safe Mode.
Intel-based Mac: Turn on or restart the Mac. Immediately press and hold the Shift key until the login window appears.

Once Safe Mode starts, turn off Wi-Fi or unplug the Ethernet cable. Then contact Apple Support or a trusted cybersecurity professional. Removing a browser extension or clearing your history will not remove ClickLock's persistent backdoor.

Use a separate trusted device to change the password for your primary email account. Then secure your Apple Account and any financial accounts stored on the Mac. Change password manager credentials and review active sessions. Sign out of devices or sessions you do not recognize. Review the devices connected to your Apple Account and remove unfamiliar ones. Apple also recommends changing your Apple Account password when you suspect unauthorized access. After a professional cleans or resets the Mac, change its local login password. Assume the attacker received that password if you entered it into the ClickLock window.
Kurt's key takeaways

ClickLock depends on one dangerous moment: convincing you to paste a command into Terminal. Once that happens, the malware can begin stealing information before the password pressure even starts. The biggest red flag is easy to remember. No trustworthy website needs Terminal to prove you are human. If your Mac starts closing apps and demanding a password, shut it down rather than giving in. Start in Safe Mode and get help checking for the persistent backdoor. Then use another trusted device to secure your most important accounts.
