The renewed optimism follows mounting fears of a return to all-out war across the Middle East, as the battle for control of the crucial Strait of Hormuz expanded to the Red Sea, another key waterway for global trade.
Trump said Thursday that he was considering a “massive attack” to try to break Iran’s grip on the strait, but since then the U.S. and Iran have refrained from attacks for three days.
The U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, Mike Waltz, told “Meet the Press” on Sunday that the decision to halt strikes came in response to ongoing talks between the two sides.

“What the president is doing right now, as we’ve seen all along, is giving some talks some space,” he said, adding that talks were “ongoing” but that there was “internal fighting” on the Iranian side.
Still, Tehran offered limited hope for any ramped-up peace efforts.

“Mediators may convey messages from the American side to us concerning regional developments, but at the present time we have no negotiations with the American side,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said today at a news conference.

title: Bryan Kohberger files a petition to challenge his guilty plea and conviction
summary: Bryan Kohberger, the man convicted of killing four University of Idaho students in 2022, is seeking to abandon his guilty plea and wants his day in court.
story: Bryan Kohberger, the man convicted of killing four University of Idaho students in 2022, is seeking to abandon his guilty plea and wants his day in court.

Kohberger, who pleaded guilty in July 2025 to avoid a quadruple murder trial and is serving four life sentences, filed a “petition for post conviction relief” Monday in the Ada County District Court in Idaho.
A petition for post-conviction relief is a way to challenge a conviction outside the appeals process. The court record indicates that Kohberger is representing himself.
It was not immediately clear on what grounds he was seeking the petition.
But in an interview with The New York Times, Kohberger claimed he is innocent and was misled into confessing to the murders.
“My actual innocence is my truth, and the plea, hinged on by false promises and blatant disinformation, MUST be withdrawn,” he said in a statement to the newspaper Sunday night.

Dismissing the state investigators’ account of what happened as a “myopic narrative” and a “work of fiction,” Kohberger said in the statement that “its faulty premises were never challenged at trial.”

“Circumnavigated by a broken plea, the trial never provided the public the clarity conducive to closure, and justice shall remain abjectly miscarried unless that plea is withdrawn,” the statement said.
Kohberger admitted last year to killing the four students — Madison Mogen, 21; Kaylee Goncalves, 21; Xana Kernodle, 20; and Ethan Chapin, 20 — at an off-campus house on Nov. 13, 2022.

A doctoral student in criminal justice at the time of the murders, Kohberger took a plea deal and was sentenced to four consecutive life sentences for four counts of first-degree murder and 10 years in prison for a burglary charge.
While he told a judge that he broke into the off-campus house in Moscow, Idaho, and killed four of the six students there, most of them as they slept, he has never said what motivated the killings.
Before the filing, Kohberger had not made any public statements suggesting he might change his plea.
Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador said his office “stands ready to do whatever is necessary to ensure justice is fully carried out.”
“My heart goes out to the families of Madison, Kaylee, Xana, and Ethan, who have already endured unimaginable loss and now must face today’s deeply painful news,” he posted on X.
The Goncalves family referred to Kohberger in a statement as “the mosquito you just can’t seem to swat” and criticized The New York Times for providing him with a platform.
“The piece had little else to offer beyond a guilty man once again claiming he is innocent,” it said.
The Goncalves family said they wanted Kohberger to face trial — and a possible death penalty. But Kohberger opted to plead guilty.

“He wants another chance to roll the dice,” the family said in the statement. “The defendant will get another day in court—a welcome break from solitary confinement: a ride, perhaps different food, photos taken, and the spotlight once again fixed on him and his supposed ‘innocence’.”

title: Trump, Congress and world leaders to honor the late Sen. Lindsey Graham in Washington
summary: World leaders, President Donald Trump and officials in Washington will pay their respects in funeral services for Republican Sen. Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham.
story: WASHINGTON — World leaders, President Donald Trump and officials in Washington will pay their respects Tuesday to Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died suddenly at age 71 this month and was one of the most prominent and influential lawmakers on Capitol Hill.
Two days of funeral services begin Tuesday in Washington and will continue Wednesday in Graham’s native South Carolina, which he represented in Congress for more than three decades.

On Tuesday morning, Graham’s casket will be carried by an armed forces body bearer team in honor of the senator’s military service; he served as an Air Force judge advocate general, or JAG, officer and retired from the Air Force Reserve in 2015 with the rank of colonel.

While Graham will not lie in state or honor, as U.S. presidents and other prominent figures have, Graham will be recognized with a special ceremony in the Capitol’s rotunda. The armed forces team will be replaced by a U.S. Capitol Police memorial guard in recognition of Graham’s service in the Senate. The brief ceremony will be private but livestreamed.

“From the military to state politics to decades of representing South Carolinians in Congress, Lindsey dedicated his life to giving back through public service,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said in a statement. “As we say our final goodbyes, it seems fitting for his friends and colleagues to give back to him through this special Capitol honor.”
After the Capitol ceremony, Graham’s casket will depart for Washington National Cathedral for an invitation-only funeral service at 2 p.m. ET, which will also be livestreamed.

Trump, who was one of the last people to speak to Graham and said he considered the senator like “family,” is expected to deliver remarks at the funeral. Cabinet officials and congressional and military leaders are also expected to be on hand.

So are global leaders who have worked closely with Graham on defense and foreign policy issues for years, including Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Trump is expected to meet separately Tuesday with Netanyahu and Zelenskyy.

Just two days after Graham’s death, South Carolina GOP Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Graham’s sister and only sibling, Darline Graham, to fill out the six months remaining in his Senate term. She announced last week that she’ll run for a full, six-year term, and she has the difficult task of planning for her brother’s services, getting up to speed on Senate business and running for a fast-approaching Aug. 11 primary election.

After the services in Washington, Graham will make his final journey to South Carolina — a flight he took hundreds of times during his eight years in the House and nearly a quarter century in the Senate.
The public is invited to pay its respects along a procession route at about 10:45 a.m. ET Wednesday at the South Carolina State House in Columbia, where Graham’s political career began in 1993.

Graham’s casket will be carried by a South Carolina State Guard horse-drawn military wagon, known as a caisson, and there will be a presentation of law enforcement from agencies across South Carolina on the north steps of the State House. An F-16 flyover from the 169th Fighter Wing from McEntire Joint National Guard Base will follow at about 11 a.m. ET.

The caisson will continue down Main Street and arrive at First Baptist Church of Columbia, where a funeral service will be held.  A private family burial will take place in Pickens County, South Carolina, where Lindsey and Darline Graham were born and raised.

Lindsey Graham, who had been chairman of the Senate Budget Committee, died the night of July 11 after emergency personnel responded to a call for “cardiac arrest” at his home near the U.S. Capitol. He had just returned from a trip to Kyiv, Ukraine, where he had met with Zelenskyy, and was expected to be a guest on NBC News’ “Meet the Press” the next morning.

Graham’s office said that the preliminary cause of death was “aortic dissection due to arteriosclerotic cardiovascular disease,” or a rupture of his aorta due to a hardening of his arteries. Results of toxicology and other tests are still pending.

title: Citing ‘common sense,’ James Comey’s team urges judge to toss seashells case
summary: Attorneys for James Comey have asked a federal judge to dismiss the seashells-based prosecution of the former FBI director.
story: Attorneys for James Comey have asked a federal judge to dismiss the seashells-based prosecution of the former FBI director, arguing that “dictionaries, context, precedent, and common sense” gut the Trump administration’s claim that a photo he posted on Instagram could possibly constitute an actual threat against President Donald Trump.

If the case were to survive the legal challenges, it would go to trial in October. Comey was indicted by a grand jury in the Eastern District of North Carolina in April. Prosecutors argued that an image he posted online of seashells grouped in the formation of the numbers “86 47” was a threat against the president. Matthew Petracca, a rookie federal prosecutor and former Republican official who first brought the case, has since moved off the case.
The term “86” is widely understood to be a restaurant term meaning to be out of something. Trump is the 47th president.

Comey’s team argued in a court filing Monday that no reasonable person aware of the relevant context would read the phrase as a suggestion of violence and that — even if it could be read that way — “a reasonable observer would still understand Mr. Comey’s post as mere political hyperbole, not a true threat.”
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google
“The Supreme Court has rejected threats prosecutions based on speech far more directly threatening than Mr. Comey’s seashells post here,” the team of eight attorneys wrote.
“Forcing Mr. Comey to stand trial for a statement opposing the President — even if he is ultimately acquitted — would itself be an unconstitutional punishment of free speech,” they wrote.
The Justice Department has until Aug. 18 to respond to Comey’s motions to dismiss the case.
Comey’s team is expected to file a motion arguing that the case is the product of selective and vindictive prosecution by Tuesday.

A federal judge in the District of Columbia separately ruled that it was “difficult to fathom how any reasonable observer” would view an “8647” flag flown by protesters on National Park Service land as a true threat. During oral arguments, the government itself conceded there were circumstances in which those numbers together wouldn’t be considered a threat against the president.
Comey has said the seashells case highlights Trump’s “bottomless desire“ for revenge.

Last year, a Trump ally who had never worked as a prosecutor before brought a separate case against Comey over congressional testimony he gave back in 2020, but a federal judge dismissed that case after ruling Lindsey Halligan was unlawfully appointed.
The lawyers argued the case is about protected free speech, and seeking to prosecute the case would only discourage free debate over politics — a tenet of American society.

Comey’s team also argued that Trump’s public pronouncements have been far more violent: The president “asserted that a video posted by several Members of Congress criticizing military policy was ‘punishable by death’ and was cause for ‘hang[ing] them’”; he remarked during the 2016 campaign that “Second Amendment people” might be the only ones who could stop Hillary Clinton if she were elected; he made comments about Rep. Liz Cheney being a “radical war hawk” and then stated, “Let’s put her with a rifle standing there with nine barrels shooting at her, OK? Let’s see how she feels about it, you know, when the guns are trained on her face.”
Comey’s attorneys also pointed to a line Trump’s legal team made as they sought to dismiss the Jan. 6, 2021, case against him.

“As the president himself has argued when he was a defendant in a criminal case, an ‘indictment must be dismissed’ where it ‘seeks to criminalize core political speech and advocacy that lies at the heart of the First Amendment,” they wrote.

title: Mitch McConnell releases health update, saying he’s not ready to return to work yet
summary: Sen. Mitch McConnell’s office released a health update Monday, saying he’s still not ready to return to in-person work after his June 14 hospitalization.
story: WASHINGTON — Sen. Mitch McConnell’s office released a health update Monday, saying he’s still not ready to return to in-person work in the Capitol after his June 14 hospitalization.

“I’m still working hard to get back to my full schedule of work in the Senate and in Kentucky, keeping up with intense physical therapy per my doctors’ orders,” McConnell, R-Ky., said in a statement. “Unfortunately, that means I won’t be able to make it to Fancy Farm, Kentucky this Saturday.”
Thune says he defers to McConnell and team on health updates

McConnell, who said he’s in rehabilitation care after a fall at his home last month, added that there’s “no place I’d rather be” than the annual picnic in Kentucky this weekend and “I hate that I’ll miss the fun this year.” He said he’s “looking forward to getting back to the Senate and to Kentucky soon.”

McConnell’s office did not provide a timeline for his return. He has missed the last 38 votes on the Senate floor, according to an NBC News review. The chamber is scheduled to be in session for the next two weeks before summer recess.
His office released a new photo of him with his wife, Elaine Chao.

McConnell’s office also released a statement from the Office of the Attending Physician, saying that the senator “continues his recovery from a fall at home in June,” adding: “He is not yet medically cleared to leave the rehab facility and return to the office.”

“Since his discharge from hospital care, he has maintained a strenuous course of physical therapy and rehabilitation, including multiple sessions a day designed to rebuild strength and reduce the risk of future falls,” the OAP statement read.

It is the first update from McConnell’s team since July 12, when he first disclosed the details of what led to his hospitalization. He said he suffered a fall and was “briefly unconscious,” but never had a heart attack or stroke, nor any tumors or hemorrhages.
McConnell is scheduled to retire when his term expires at the end of this Congress, as he isn’t running for re-election in November.

title: Wife of Kansas City Chiefs OC Eric Bieniemy allegedly shot by their son
summary: The wife of Kansas City Chiefs offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy was shot on Sunday night in Northern Virginia, allegedly by their son, authorities said.
story: The wife of Kansas City Chiefs offensive coordinator Eric  Bieniemy was shot on Sunday night in Northern Virginia, allegedly by their son, authorities said.
Loudon County Sheriff’s deputies found a woman “suffering from multiple gunshot wounds” in the 2000 block of Northpark Drive in the Washington, D.C., suburb of Ashburn, officials said.

Elijah Zion Bieniemy, 27, was arrested and booked on suspicion of malicious wounding, use of a firearm in commission of a felony, and discharge of a firearm inside of a dwelling, according to a sheriff’s statement.
He was booked into the Loudoun County Adult Detention Center and held without bond. There “is not believed to be any threat to the public,” according to the sheriff.
The Chiefs are in preseason training at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph, Missouri.
“She’s a saint,” Kansas City Chiefs coach Andy Reid told reporters on Monday, calling Mia Bieniemy “one of God’s good blessings.”
“But the fact that she’s in stable condition, I think is a positive for what it could be.”
The team’s passing game coordinator, Joe Bleymaier, and offensive line coach, Andy Heck, will expand their duties while Bieniemy attends to his injured wife, according to Reid.

“The club is aware of the incident involving Eric Bieniemy’s family,” Chiefs spokesperson Brad Gee said on Monday. “Out of respect for their privacy, we won’t have a comment at this time. Our thoughts and prayers are with them.”
The elder Bieniemy, 56, is in his second stint as Chiefs offensive coordinator. He ran the K.C. offense from 2018 to 2022, coaching in three Super Bowls during that span.

He went on to run the offense for the Washington Commanders and UCLA Bruins before serving as running backs coach for the Chicago Bears in 2025 before returning to his previous position with the Chiefs.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

title: Secret Service agent charged in near-fatal hazing that led to victim’s kidney failure
summary: A Secret Service agent in Florida and two others were arrested in connection to a brutal, dayslong college hazing ritual that nearly ended in a victim’s death, officials said Sunday.
story: A Secret Service agent in Florida and two others were arrested in connection to a brutal, dayslong college hazing ritual that nearly ended in a victim’s death, officials said Sunday.

Marquez Christopher Pinder, 29, was placed on administrative leave, and the Secret Service is “fully cooperating with the investigation,” according to a statement by Special Agent in Charge Michael Townsend, who runs the agency’s Miami field office.

Pinder, Jared Lamar James, 26, and Elijah Delano Dyous, 29, have also been booked on suspicion of attempted manslaughter with a deadly weapon, aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and hazing with a deadly weapon, according to the Miami-Dade State Attorney’s Office.

Two pledges, identified only as Victim 1 and Victim 2, were “subjected to severe beatings,” according to an arrest warrant written by Sweetwater police Detective Kevin Espinosa and Miami-Dade County Sheriff’s Detective Alejandro Venturin.

Victim 1 was identified as a former undergraduate student at the University of Miami in Coral Gables who was seeking membership at Kappa Alpha Psi, according to the arrest warrant. Victim 1 is now a grad student at the University of Miami, officials said.
Victim 2 was called “another prospective pledge” in the warrant.
While Pinder was called “dean of pledges” in the arrest warrant, the university said he has no connection to the Coral Gables campus or that chapter of the fraternity.
“The agent, Marquez Christopher Pinder is in no way affiliated with the University of Miami or the University’s undergraduate chapter of Kappa Alpha Psi,” according to a university statement.
It wasn’t immediately clear how or why the 29-year-old Pinder would have such intimate connections to a college frat.

“An investigation revealed evidence of alleged hazing incidents involving prolonged and repeated beatings with canes and paddles,” prosecutors said in a statement. “A failure to correctly answer questions about the fraternity allegedly led to the beatings.”
The alleged hazing began inside an apartment April 1 in Sweetwater, Florida, and continued into April 2 and 3 at that location, prosecutors said.
The hazing kept going into April 4, at a residence in unincorporated Miami-Dade County, officials said.
The beatings caused Victim 1 to have to receive “extensive skin grafts” to his backside that had been “blackened by the presence of necrotic skin/tissue,” according to the arrest warrant.

That victim “continues to suffer from extreme pain and discomfort as a result of the” alleged beatings, the warrant said, with prosecutors saying he suffered kidney failure that could have been fatal.
“Additionally, ‘Victim 1’s’ mobility and quality of life have been significantly impacted,” according to the arrest warrant.
Victim 2 told investigators he was not a hazing victim but admitted to seeking medical care for injuries to his backside in April, officials said.

“These external and internal injuries mirrored those suffered by ‘Victim 1’ and were consistent with the statement provided by ‘Victim  1’ that ‘Victim 2’ was subjected to severe beatings to his backside,” the arrest warrant said.
All three suspects were in custody Monday.
The suspects are not current students and have no authority to act in fraternity affairs, according to the frat’s national president, Jimmy McMikle.

“Kappa Alpha Psi is a non-hazing fraternity. We neither condone nor tolerate acts of hazing behavior within our organization or from our membership,” McMikle said in a statement to NBC News on Monday.

“They do not have an official affiliation with any chapter nor any official role with the organization. Likewise, they do not have any authority to conduct any program or authorize any process on our behalf. We have and will continue to cooperate fully with law enforcement as they conduct their investigation to help with the administration of justice as it should unfold.”

While hazing “might be seen as a tradition creating a sense of belonging and brotherhood,” State Attorney Katherine Fernandez Rundle said those acts amount to crimes with victims in “graves and in hospital beds.”
It wasn’t immediately clear if Pinder, James and Dyous had hired or been assigned attorneys to speak on their behalf.

story: Flats are stylish and can certainly be more comfortable than heels, but they are not without their own issues. The problem often lies in the very name of this style of shoe. A completely flat shoe means no support — particularly arch support, which goes a long way when it comes to keeping your feet comfortable and stable.

“Arch support keeps your foot better aligned, which helps support your entire body and makes sure there is good distribution of pressure across your feet,” says Dr. Gregory Alvarez, a podiatrist at the Ankle and Foot Centers of America. That even distribution matters more than you might think — when weight isn’t spread properly across your foot, it puts extra strain further up the chain, in your muscles, ligaments and joints.

The good news is that there are flats out there that offer that much-needed arch support. To help you find flats that actually do right by your feet, I asked podiatrists what to look for and rounded up the pairs worth adding to your shoe rotation.

Podiatrists have previously recommended Birkenstocks to me as a go-to brand for walking sandals because they offer a supportive, contoured footbed with built-in arch support. These ballet flat-style shoes cradle your arch and heel the way most flats never do, plus have a strap that goes across the top of your foot to keep your foot from sliding around.
How I picked the best flats with arch support
To select the best flats with arch support, I asked experts what to consider while shopping. Here are the things they suggest you prioritize:

Support: Look for a raised section in the middle of your insole — almost like a mini hill. This will tell you that the shoe has built-in arch support. Additionally, look for a flat that cups your heel to keep your foot in place. This ensures your foot doesn’t move around and helps you stay steady on your feet. Limited bendability: Before you buy a pair of flats, consider trying a bend test. Here’s how to do it: Try bending the sole in half. You want it to be able to bend it at the ball of the foot, not at the midfoot, says Landau. Firmness from the midfoot to the heel means the shoe is more supportive, while bending at the ball gives you enough flexibility to be comfortable.Heel drop: You want your flats to be, well, flat — but too flat could cause issues. That’s where a heel drop comes in. Heel drop is the height difference between the heel and the forefoot of a shoe; you want the back of the shoe to be slightly more elevated than the front of the shoe. “This matches the foot anatomy more and reduces stress on your feet,” says Landau. “In turn, this will reduce pain and soreness.” That said, finding a decent heel drop in a flat can be difficult. Ideally, a heel drop between 7 and 10 millimeters is ideal — but you won’t find that in most flats. So, the experts I spoke with suggested aiming for 3 millimeters, which should be easier to find.

“Wearing flats that aren’t supportive can lead to pain in the arch, plantar heel, posterior heel and ball of foot,” says Landau. “It can also cause knee, low back and hip pain.” In turn, this can lead to conditions like achilles tendonitis and plantar fasciitis, which are inflammation issues that can cause ongoing pain.

Yes, you can absolutely add insoles to your flats. Many flats do not have arch support and there are plenty of insoles out there that do not take up too much room in sleeker styles of flats, says Landau, who says she often adds her own custom insoles to her flats. title: Citing ‘common sense,’ James Comey’s team urges judge to toss seashells case
summary: Attorneys for James Comey have asked a federal judge to dismiss the seashells-based prosecution of the former FBI director.
story: Attorneys for James Comey have asked a federal judge to dismiss the seashells-based prosecution of the former FBI director, arguing that “dictionaries, context, precedent, and common sense” gut the Trump administration’s claim that a photo he posted on Instagram could possibly constitute an actual threat against President Donald Trump.

If the case were to survive the legal challenges, it would go to trial in October. Comey was indicted by a grand jury in the Eastern District of North Carolina in April. Prosecutors argued that an image he posted online of seashells grouped in the formation of the numbers “86 47” was a threat against the president. Matthew Petracca, a rookie federal prosecutor and former Republican official who first brought the case, has since moved off the case.
The term “86” is widely understood to be a restaurant term meaning to be out of something. Trump is the 47th president.

Comey’s team argued in a court filing Monday that no reasonable person aware of the relevant context would read the phrase as a suggestion of violence and that — even if it could be read that way — “a reasonable observer would still understand Mr. Comey’s post as mere political hyperbole, not a true threat.”
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google
“The Supreme Court has rejected threats prosecutions based on speech far more directly threatening than Mr. Comey’s seashells post here,” the team of eight attorneys wrote.
“Forcing Mr. Comey to stand trial for a statement opposing the President — even if he is ultimately acquitted — would itself be an unconstitutional punishment of free speech,” they wrote.
The Justice Department has until Aug. 18 to respond to Comey’s motions to dismiss the case.
Comey’s team is expected to file a motion arguing that the case is the product of selective and vindictive prosecution by Tuesday.

A federal judge in the District of Columbia separately ruled that it was “difficult to fathom how any reasonable observer” would view an “8647” flag flown by protesters on National Park Service land as a true threat. During oral arguments, the government itself conceded there were circumstances in which those numbers together wouldn’t be considered a threat against the president.
Comey has said the seashells case highlights Trump’s “bottomless desire“ for revenge.

Last year, a Trump ally who had never worked as a prosecutor before brought a separate case against Comey over congressional testimony he gave back in 2020, but a federal judge dismissed that case after ruling Lindsey Halligan was unlawfully appointed.
The lawyers argued the case is about protected free speech, and seeking to prosecute the case would only discourage free debate over politics — a tenet of American society.

Comey’s team also argued that Trump’s public pronouncements have been far more violent: The president “asserted that a video posted by several Members of Congress criticizing military policy was ‘punishable by death’ and was cause for ‘hang[ing] them’”; he remarked during the 2016 campaign that “Second Amendment people” might be the only ones who could stop Hillary Clinton if she were elected; he made comments about Rep. Liz Cheney being a “radical war hawk” and then stated, “Let’s put her with a rifle standing there with nine barrels shooting at her, OK? Let’s see how she feels about it, you know, when the guns are trained on her face.”
Comey’s attorneys also pointed to a line Trump’s legal team made as they sought to dismiss the Jan. 6, 2021, case against him.

“As the president himself has argued when he was a defendant in a criminal case, an ‘indictment must be dismissed’ where it ‘seeks to criminalize core political speech and advocacy that lies at the heart of the First Amendment,” they wrote.

title: Trump, Congress and world leaders to honor the late Sen. Lindsey Graham in Washington
summary: World leaders, President Donald Trump and officials in Washington will pay their respects in funeral services for Republican Sen. Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham.
story: WASHINGTON — World leaders, President Donald Trump and officials in Washington will pay their respects Tuesday to Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died suddenly at age 71 this month and was one of the most prominent and influential lawmakers on Capitol Hill.
Two days of funeral services begin Tuesday in Washington and will continue Wednesday in Graham’s native South Carolina, which he represented in Congress for more than three decades.

On Tuesday morning, Graham’s casket will be carried by an armed forces body bearer team in honor of the senator’s military service; he served as an Air Force judge advocate general, or JAG, officer and retired from the Air Force Reserve in 2015 with the rank of colonel.

While Graham will not lie in state or honor, as U.S. presidents and other prominent figures have, Graham will be recognized with a special ceremony in the Capitol’s rotunda. The armed forces team will be replaced by a U.S. Capitol Police memorial guard in recognition of Graham’s service in the Senate. The brief ceremony will be private but livestreamed.

“From the military to state politics to decades of representing South Carolinians in Congress, Lindsey dedicated his life to giving back through public service,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said in a statement. “As we say our final goodbyes, it seems fitting for his friends and colleagues to give back to him through this special Capitol honor.”
After the Capitol ceremony, Graham’s casket will depart for Washington National Cathedral for an invitation-only funeral service at 2 p.m. ET, which will also be livestreamed.

Trump, who was one of the last people to speak to Graham and said he considered the senator like “family,” is expected to deliver remarks at the funeral. Cabinet officials and congressional and military leaders are also expected to be on hand.

So are global leaders who have worked closely with Graham on defense and foreign policy issues for years, including Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Trump is expected to meet separately Tuesday with Netanyahu and Zelenskyy.

Just two days after Graham’s death, South Carolina GOP Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Graham’s sister and only sibling, Darline Graham, to fill out the six months remaining in his Senate term. She announced last week that she’ll run for a full, six-year term, and she has the difficult task of planning for her brother’s services, getting up to speed on Senate business and running for a fast-approaching Aug. 11 primary election.

After the services in Washington, Graham will make his final journey to South Carolina — a flight he took hundreds of times during his eight years in the House and nearly a quarter century in the Senate.
The public is invited to pay its respects along a procession route at about 10:45 a.m. ET Wednesday at the South Carolina State House in Columbia, where Graham’s political career began in 1993.

Graham’s casket will be carried by a South Carolina State Guard horse-drawn military wagon, known as a caisson, and there will be a presentation of law enforcement from agencies across South Carolina on the north steps of the State House. An F-16 flyover from the 169th Fighter Wing from McEntire Joint National Guard Base will follow at about 11 a.m. ET.

The caisson will continue down Main Street and arrive at First Baptist Church of Columbia, where a funeral service will be held.  A private family burial will take place in Pickens County, South Carolina, where Lindsey and Darline Graham were born and raised.

Lindsey Graham, who had been chairman of the Senate Budget Committee, died the night of July 11 after emergency personnel responded to a call for “cardiac arrest” at his home near the U.S. Capitol. He had just returned from a trip to Kyiv, Ukraine, where he had met with Zelenskyy, and was expected to be a guest on NBC News’ “Meet the Press” the next morning.

Graham’s office said that the preliminary cause of death was “aortic dissection due to arteriosclerotic cardiovascular disease,” or a rupture of his aorta due to a hardening of his arteries. Results of toxicology and other tests are still pending.

title: Sen. John Hoffman says Angie Craig sought his endorsement while he was in ICU
summary: Democratic Minnesota state Sen. John Hoffman said Rep. Angie Craig, D-Minn., sought his endorsement for her Senate campaign while he was in intensive care following the June 2025 attempt on his life.
story: Democratic Minnesota state Sen. John Hoffman said Friday that Rep. Angie Craig, D-Minn., sought his endorsement for her U.S. Senate campaign while he was in intensive care following the June 2025 attempt on his life.

Hoffman said in a statement to NBC News on Sunday that a “dear and trusted friend” approached him for an endorsement twice — once while he was in the intensive care unit and the second time while he was recovering at home — and that the friend “confirmed that the endorsement requests came from Congresswoman Craig.”
Hoffman’s remarks came at a campaign event for Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, who is also seeking the Democratic Senate nomination.

“When [Craig] said she wanted my endorsement, she was doing that during moments when our family’s story had high visibility, and that’s all you need to know that the difference is between the opponent that Peggy has and Peggy Flanagan. Because Peggy Flanagan, she checked on us out of her love for how we were doing and if we were OK,” Hoffman said at a rally Friday in St. Paul, at which Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., was also present.
Asked about the allegations, a spokesperson for Flanagan said, “That’s a matter between Congresswoman Craig and the Hoffmans.”
A spokesperson for Craig said in a statement that “the claim is categorically false.”

“The Congresswoman reached out to Senator Hoffman only expressing deep sympathy from her and her wife, Cheryl, after their horrific shooting while he was in the ICU and did not reach out again until August 5, after he began making political endorsements in other races again,” the spokesperson said. “The Congresswoman continues to pray and keeps John, Yvette and Hope Hoffman in her thoughts and is grateful for their continued recovery.”
Craig denied Hoffman’s claims in an interview with KMSP-TV of Minneapolis, to which Hoffman responded in his statement.
“Let me be equally clear: I told the truth about what Yvette and I experienced,” Hoffman said about himself and his wife, who was also shot during the assassination attempt.

In text messages the Craig campaign provided to NBC News, Craig expresses well-wishes for the Hoffmans on June 14 — the day of the shooting — and she later sends an Aug. 5 message saying she “would love to talk with you about the open Senate race when you’re up to it.”
Hoffman was released from the intensive care unit on July 7.
NBC News has made attempts to contact and confirm the identity of the “dear and trusted friend” Hoffman referred to in his statement as having visited him in the intensive care unit.

Hoffman added in his statement that he “acknowledged” Craig sent a message expressing sympathy following the shooting, but he said his campaign remarks were in reference to subsequent endorsement requests “and the painful impression those requests left on our family while we were trying to survive and recover.”
“It is dishonest to give condolences and then immediately ask for endorsement like her text showed,” Hoffman wrote.

State Sen. Erin Maye Quade said in an interview with NBC News on Sunday that when she visited Hoffman at the intensive care unit rehabilitation facility in late July, he shared the story about someone seeking an endorsement on behalf of Craig.

“He had mentioned that there was a friend of his that had come, who was also a surrogate and working with Angie’s campaign, and had asked him for his endorsement. We were both like, ‘Oh, it’s so inappropriate,’ and he was like: ‘I know. I think he felt really bad about doing it,’” Quade said, adding that the story has not been “secret or private” since then and that Hoffman has mentioned it to other people “at various points over the last year.”
Hoffman added in his statement Sunday that Flanagan’s contact with the Hoffmans was “different” and said she had reached out to check in on the family and “sought nothing in return.”

“My remarks were about that contrast, and I remain accountable for every word I said,” Hoffman wrote. “Congresswoman Craig may disagree with my endorsement. She may defend her campaign’s conduct. But she does not get to rewrite what my family experienced or publicly attack my honesty.”

Vance Boelter, 59, pleaded guilty last month to six federal counts in connection with the stalking and shooting of the Hoffmans, in addition to the murders of House Speaker Emerita Melissa Hortman and her husband, Mark Hortman. Boelter was sentenced to two consecutive terms of life in prison and an additional 40 years, the maximum sentence short of the death penalty.

title: Mike Waltz dismisses concerns over depleted U.S. weapons stockpile amid Iran war
summary: The United Nations ambassador said the U.S. has “everything that it needs” for military operations against Iran.
story: Mike Waltz, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” Sunday that the U.S. has “everything that it needs” for military operations against Iran, dismissing reporting that U.S. weapons stockpiles are depleted.

“I want to be crystal clear: The U.S. military, and I’ve verified this every which way, has everything that it needs to conduct this campaign as effectively as it needs to be,” he said. “And I have to tell you, the people that are leaking this nonsense deserve to be in jail.”

He was responding to questions about an NBC News report that U.S. military commanders are allowing some Iranian attacks through U.S. defenses as part of an effort to preserve the Pentagon’s weapons supply, according to two senior U.S. officials.
NBC News has also previously reported that U.S. weapons stockpiles are diminishing as the war with Iran continues.
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google
Waltz initially argued that stockpiles were depleted during the Biden administration.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth “inherited a depleted situation from not only Ukraine, but also the ongoing fight with the Houthis under the Biden administration and a depleted military under the Biden administration,” Waltz said.

The military under the Trump administration, he said, has decided that “one, they’re going to new types of munitions, cheaper munitions, new technologies, but also with these new defense budgets, rebuilding our great military.”
The White House and the Pentagon didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Hegseth appeared before lawmakers last week to ask for $67 billion in supplemental funding to expand production and speed up delivery of weapons.
During a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing in April, Hegseth acknowledged in an exchange with Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., that it could take “months and years” to rebuild the weapons stockpile.
In a separate interview with “Meet the Press” moderator Kristen Welker, Kelly referred to that exchange, saying that the situation was “by their own making.”
“They’re not keeping track,” Kelly said. “They, at this point, this president and the people around him are incompetent.”
Asked whether he would vote to approve the supplemental funding, Kelly said he has not yet made a final decision.

“If we had some competent people running this department, you could figure out, how do you defend our nation in a way and give the troops what they need within a reasonable budget?” he said earlier. “What they’re asking for is not reasonable.”

In recent days, the U.S. launched nearly two weeks of consecutive nightly attacks on Iran. Trump has told reporters that the U.S. is still “talking to them,” but Iran and its proxies have continued strikes on ships, snarling global trading routes.
Asked whether Trump has decided against escalation amid the pause in consecutive strikes, Waltz said he “wouldn’t go that far at all,” adding that “the president is keeping all options on the table.”
“What the president is doing right now, as we’ve seen all along, is giving some talks some space,” Waltz said. “Talks are ongoing; they’re happening at every level.”

On Saturday, a journalist for the French media outlet LCI reported that she asked Trump whether he was considering resuming full-scale war with Iran. She said Trump replied that “if we don’t get 100% of what we want, absolutely.”

title: Democrats pick Troy Jackson to replace Graham Platner in must-win Maine Senate race
summary: Former state Senate President Troy Jackson officially became Democrats’ Senate nominee in Maine Saturday, starting a 101-day sprint to Election Day in a nationally watched, must-win race for his party.
story: BANGOR, Maine — Former state Senate President Troy Jackson officially became Democrats’ Senate nominee in Maine, starting a 101-day sprint to Election Day in a nationally watched, must-win race for his party.

Hundreds of Democrats gathered in Bangor on Saturday morning for a state convention to pick their Senate nominee after the primary winner, Graham Platner, ended his campaign earlier this month after a sexual assault allegation, which he denied.
Jackson, a veteran legislator, was expected to win the nod after delegate candidates supporting him dominated at county meetings last weekend and all of his major opponents dropped out.
And Democrats are eager to move on to the general election.

“I officially call this convention to order — with a sigh of relief,” Maine Democratic Party Chair Charlie Dingman told the Democrats packed into a ballroom. Dingman announced later Saturday morning that Jackson had captured all but five of the 571 ballots cast at the convention, prompting roars from the crowd and chants of “Troy! Troy! Troy!”

The rapid series of events has shaken the Maine contest, where longtime Sen. Susan Collins, the only Republican representing a state President Donald Trump lost in 2024, is seeking a sixth term. Democrats are looking to net four seats and take control of the Senate this fall, and Maine represents one of their best opportunities to notch a win, at least on paper. If Democrats do not defeat Collins, they’ll have to pick up another seat in a state Trump carried by double digits.
Jackson previewed his case against the senator at Saturday’s convention.

“For nearly 30 years, Collins has told Maine that she is concerned,” Jackson said. “She was concerned while she rubber-stamped Trump’s Medicaid cuts and gutted our healthcare. She’s concerned when she cut taxes for corporations and the wealthy. Concerned when she confirmed justices who overturned Roe v. Wade, and really tragically, she was concerned when she gave ICE billions to terrorize our neighbors and murder people in the streets with no accountability.”

“But concern does not lower the costs of groceries or gas. Concern does not keep our monitoring wards of rural hospitals like down in Lincoln County open. Concern does not restore all the rights that she’s taken away,” Jackson continued.
“Maine does not need another six years of concern.” he added. “We need someone with courage. We need a fighter, and we need a senator who remembers exactly who sent them to Washington.”
The Collins campaign criticized Jackson’s candidacy as “low-energy” and the product of a closed process run by Democratic Party elites.

“Today, in a process concocted by the Maine Democratic Party establishment, a 24-year Augusta insider was appointed to run for the Senate by fewer than three-tenths of one percent of its primary voters,” Collins campaign spokesman Shawn Roderick said in a statement, adding: “Our campaign will continue to run on Senator Collins’ bipartisan record of delivering results for Maine and America, which will stand in stark contrast to Troy’s low-energy campaign and his partisan record of driving up costs, hurting our schools, and making life less affordable for families across the state.”
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google
As his focus turns to Collins, Jackson must confront several daunting tasks, and with no time to spare.
He has to not only build a statewide campaign. He has to raise millions of dollars to compete on the airwaves.
Most of all, he has to convince huge numbers of Mainers who have repeatedly backed Collins for decades that it’s time for her to go.
Jackson’s path to victory
Many Democrats backed Jackson’s bid because they saw him as the candidate with the best chance of defeating Collins in November.

Supporters of Jackson, a former logger and longtime legislator from Allagash, a tiny town at the northern tip of the state, believe he will have unique appeal to working-class voters and cut into Collins’ margins in rural Maine. It’s the first time Collins, from Aroostook County, will be facing an opponent who also hails from the same sprawling area.
“The working class has been left behind and forgotten about,” said Shelly Mountain, a former Aroostook County Democratic Committee chairwoman and a pro-Jackson delegate at the convention.
“He is definitely working class and always — has always,” she emphasized again, “been a champion for the working class.”

A Democratic strategist with experience in Maine races, granted anonymity to speak candidly about the race and Jackson’s potential challenges, noted that a Democratic statewide win against Collins involves narrowing a likely loss in the rural 2nd Congressional District to high single digits.

“Being from Aroostook County and having shown a pretty significant overperformance in his state Senate races, [Jackson] is well-suited to do that,” the strategist said, later adding: “Of course, Sen. Collins is not a pushover. She’s done very well over the state but also particularly the 2nd District.”
Other Democrats noted that Jackson mainly has to run up the score in traditionally Democratic strongholds of Portland and other cities.

“There’s a path without expanding the map,” said David Farmer, a Maine Democratic strategist. He noted that Collins’ 2020 opponent, former state House Speaker Sara Gideon, underperformed the Democratic presidential ticket in Portland and other blue areas, due in part to a third-party candidate.
Farmer was optimistic that this year, Democrats would stay united.
“The reactions to Trump, to the ICE killing in Biddeford, to high prices, to the war [with Iran] — that solidifies Democrats so they’re less likely to drift than in 2020,” Farmer said.

But the Democratic strategist noted that when Jackson ran in the party’s primary for governor earlier this year, he struggled in more affluent parts of the state where Collins has performed well, even as they have shifted away from the GOP in the Trump era.
“He’ll need to do better in the greater Portland suburbs,” the strategist said.
The 2020 election provides some clues about Jackson’s challenges ahead. That year, Collins won re-election nearly 9 points even as Joe Biden carried the state by the same margin.

Exit polls show that Collins overperformed with independents, moderates and women. Independents who voted for Biden by 24 points also voted for Collins by 3 points. Self-identified moderates swung 24 points for Biden, but they voted for Collins by 7 points.

Women, who have long been key to Collins’ victories, broke for Biden by 23 points, but they voted for Collins by 3 points. Collins overperformed among women who didn’t go to college and limited the margin of defeat among white women with college degrees, one of Democrats’ strongest constituencies.
More challenges ahead

Jackson’s most immediate challenge is fundraising. His campaign announced Wednesday that it had raised over $600,000 in roughly 72 hours, surpassing $1 million since launching his Senate run on July 8. Collins’ campaign had $11 million to spend as of June 30, and Republican groups are gearing up to spend millions more.
Asked if he has enough money to win the race, Jackson said with a laugh, “Well not now, but I hope to get it,” adding that he’ll have the resources to prevail “because we got the right message.”
Jackson is likely to get outside help, too, as Democratic groups that had abandoned Platner amid his scandals re-engage in the race.

Ahead of the convention, Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., the chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, signaled that Jackson could expect full support from the deep-pocketed party apparatus once he clinched the nomination.
“We’re excited for Maine,” Gillibrand said, adding that after state Democrats “finish their primary,” the DSCC will “support whoever wins.”
Jackson said Saturday that he has not spoken with any Democratic senators, and had not yet spoken with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y.
Republicans, meanwhile, are gearing up to unload attacks on Jackson, particularly over his long tenure in the state Legislature and his ties to Platner.

Senate Leadership Fund, a GOP super PAC, is launching a new six-figure ad campaign aimed at Jackson, starting with a digital ad launching on Saturday. The group has plans to spend more than $42 million on the race.

The ad highlights recent headlines on Jackson’s temper and heated confrontations with legislative colleagues, with a narrator saying, “A volatile personality, anger issues with women, verbal abuse. It’s not Graham Platner, it’s Troy Jackson. Jackson has a history of conflicts with women, bullying, even intimidation.”
“I disagree,” Jackson said when asked about the ad after the convention on Saturday.

“I am passionate about those issues. I mean, there’s just no doubt about it,” Jackson said, later adding: “Anyone that I may have argued with, that I might have went too far or got too passionate. I apologize to. But I don’t have a problem with anyone in the Legislature and the U.S. Senate.”
Jackson’s supporters were not concerned about those attacks.

“If I had been going through the same bulls--- argument about stripping people’s coverage for their medications, I’d be throwing f-----g water bottles too,” said McGinley Jones, a 56-year-old small-business owner and convention delegate from Washington County, referring to an episode where Jackson reportedly threw a water bottle during a meeting on prescription drug legislation.

“I’m all for him getting passionate,” said Jim Gerritsen, an organic farmer representing Aroostook County at the convention, who has worked with Jackson on some pieces of legislation. “I’m all for him getting strong to fight for us because we know for sure that Susan Collins has never lifted a finger in her life to fight for the working class.”
Jackson and Platner were close allies and campaigned together, although Jackson quickly called on Platner to step aside following the sexual assault allegation.

Lance Dutson, a GOP strategist in Maine who worked on Collins’ past campaigns but is not involved in the race, suggested the contest resets without Platner, whose viral videos and impassioned critiques of the political and economic systems catapulted him to national fame.
With a “generic Democrat” as her opponent, Dutson predicted the contest would focus instead on their legislative records.

“People are going to be able to put his record up against Collins’ record. And there’s really no comparison between the two,” Dutson said, noting that Collins can point to “literally billions and billions of dollars” she has brought to Maine as a longtime member, and now chairwoman, of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee.
Collins herself has already started to try and define Jackson as out of step with Mainers.

She told NBC News earlier this week that Jackson “seems to be firmly aligned with the democratic socialists,” and she recently told CNN that Jackson is a “Bernie bro,” referring to his support for Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., during the 2016 presidential primary.

Sanders, who endorsed both Jackson and Platner in their primaries, stayed out of the brief race to pick a new Senate nominee. But he praised Jackson this week as someone who “understands the problems of the working class in Maine and throughout this country.”
Dutson, the GOP consultant, acknowledged that Jackson could have some appeal in rural parts of the state given his roots in northern Maine, but said his policies were still too far left.
“If you’re from Aroostook County, Maine, but you’re standing onstage with Bernie Sanders, that’s just a massive disconnect,” Dutson said.

One reason Democrats are relieved is Jackson wins them back voters like Carol Eisenberg, a lawyer based in Maine, who supported Janet Mills in the primary and was leery of Platner after he won the nomination.
Jackson “has my full support,” she said. “I would never cast a ballot for Susan Collins. I just wasn’t sure if I would be able to cast one for Platner.”

title: North Carolina woman vanishes after swim on Grenada beach vacation
summary: Elizabeth Waddell, 44, of Cary, was last seen at Grand Anse Beach on Wednesday, the Royal Grenada Police Force said in a missing person alert issued Thursday.
story: An American woman disappeared on vacation in Grenada, and her loved ones are pleading for help finding her.
Elizabeth “Liz” Waddell, 44, of Cary, North Carolina, was last seen at Grand Anse Beach on Wednesday, the Royal Grenada Police Force said in a missing person alert issued Thursday.
She had been staying at Grand Anse, a popular tourist destination known for its white sand and turquoise water, in St. George’s, the nation’s capital.
Police asked fishermen, boat operators and residents along the southern coastline to report any sightings of Waddell. She is described as being of medium build with short blond hair.
A spokesperson said the State Department is aware of reports that Waddell is missing in Grenada.

Her husband, Cailen Waddell, pleaded for help on Facebook. “Liz went missing in the afternoon on Wednesday. I am on my way there now to help search. I expect nothing less than Liz’s safe return — so please send your love, light, thoughts, and prayers our way,” he wrote.
Anyone with information on Waddell’s whereabouts is asked to contact the South Saint George Police Station.
Waddell is the founder of Art of Movement Physical Therapy.

She was vacationing with a friend, and the two were staying at an Airbnb property when Waddell went for a swim and did not return, Amanda Romano-Harmon, a longtime friend of Waddell and spokesperson for her family, told NBC News.

“Last Wednesday, while her friend was actually in the Airbnb finishing up an online class, Liz went ahead and put a swimsuit on and grabbed a towel and went out. They had a pool at the Airbnb, and it was very close to the beach in Grand Anse Bay, that area,” she said, recounting what she had heard from Waddell’s husband. “The friend saw her go out and put the towel out and sit down and just kind of was chilling. ... When she finished up her class, she looked out and she didn’t see Liz, so she just went outside and looked around.”
But Waddell was nowhere in sight.
“She didn’t really see her at the beach, but she did find her towel on the pier,” Romano-Harmon said.

She said Waddell went out with her swimsuit and towel and had left her phone and ID at the Airbnb. When a few hours passed without her return, the friend called Waddell’s husband and filed a missing persons report.
The police, she said, “took it seriously right from the very beginning and started deploying resources to find her.”
The last sighting of Waddell was between noon and 1 p.m. Wednesday. She was seen on a camera of a bar and grill that faces toward the pier, Romano-Harmon said.
“They did see her on the pier and getting into the water, and she was just kind of swimming and floating along, but then she floated off the camera’s view,” she said.
Romano-Harmon called Waddell’s disappearance “baffling.”
“Where is she? The Coast Guard has been out for several days. They’ve had divers out for several days. They can’t find her,” she said.
Romano-Harmon has known Waddell for almost 25 years, and her husband and Waddell’s husband were college roommates.
She described Waddell as a “ray of sunshine” and an experienced traveler who loves meeting new people.
Waddell’s adult daughter, husband and twin sister, as well as other friends, have flown to the island to aid in the search, Romano-Harmon said.
Waddell’s family, she said, is “pretty broken up.”
“They’re struggling, they want answers, and they’re trying their best,” she said.

title: Secret Service agent charged in near-fatal hazing that led to victim’s kidney failure
summary: A Secret Service agent in Florida and two others were arrested in connection to a brutal, dayslong college hazing ritual that nearly ended in a victim’s death, officials said Sunday.
story: A Secret Service agent in Florida and two others were arrested in connection to a brutal, dayslong college hazing ritual that nearly ended in a victim’s death, officials said Sunday.

Marquez Christopher Pinder, 29, was placed on administrative leave, and the Secret Service is “fully cooperating with the investigation,” according to a statement by Special Agent in Charge Michael Townsend, who runs the agency’s Miami field office.

Pinder, Jared Lamar James, 26, and Elijah Delano Dyous, 29, have also been booked on suspicion of attempted manslaughter with a deadly weapon, aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and hazing with a deadly weapon, according to the Miami-Dade State Attorney’s Office.

Two pledges, identified only as Victim 1 and Victim 2, were “subjected to severe beatings,” according to an arrest warrant written by Sweetwater police Detective Kevin Espinosa and Miami-Dade County Sheriff’s Detective Alejandro Venturin.

Victim 1 was identified as a former undergraduate student at the University of Miami in Coral Gables who was seeking membership at Kappa Alpha Psi, according to the arrest warrant. Victim 1 is now a grad student at the University of Miami, officials said.
Victim 2 was called “another prospective pledge” in the warrant.
While Pinder was called “dean of pledges” in the arrest warrant, the university said he has no connection to the Coral Gables campus or that chapter of the fraternity.
“The agent, Marquez Christopher Pinder is in no way affiliated with the University of Miami or the University’s undergraduate chapter of Kappa Alpha Psi,” according to a university statement.
It wasn’t immediately clear how or why the 29-year-old Pinder would have such intimate connections to a college frat.

“An investigation revealed evidence of alleged hazing incidents involving prolonged and repeated beatings with canes and paddles,” prosecutors said in a statement. “A failure to correctly answer questions about the fraternity allegedly led to the beatings.”
The alleged hazing began inside an apartment April 1 in Sweetwater, Florida, and continued into April 2 and 3 at that location, prosecutors said.
The hazing kept going into April 4, at a residence in unincorporated Miami-Dade County, officials said.
The beatings caused Victim 1 to have to receive “extensive skin grafts” to his backside that had been “blackened by the presence of necrotic skin/tissue,” according to the arrest warrant.

That victim “continues to suffer from extreme pain and discomfort as a result of the” alleged beatings, the warrant said, with prosecutors saying he suffered kidney failure that could have been fatal.
“Additionally, ‘Victim 1’s’ mobility and quality of life have been significantly impacted,” according to the arrest warrant.
Victim 2 told investigators he was not a hazing victim but admitted to seeking medical care for injuries to his backside in April, officials said.

“These external and internal injuries mirrored those suffered by ‘Victim 1’ and were consistent with the statement provided by ‘Victim  1’ that ‘Victim 2’ was subjected to severe beatings to his backside,” the arrest warrant said.
All three suspects were in custody Monday.
The suspects are not current students and have no authority to act in fraternity affairs, according to the frat’s national president, Jimmy McMikle.

“Kappa Alpha Psi is a non-hazing fraternity. We neither condone nor tolerate acts of hazing behavior within our organization or from our membership,” McMikle said in a statement to NBC News on Monday.

“They do not have an official affiliation with any chapter nor any official role with the organization. Likewise, they do not have any authority to conduct any program or authorize any process on our behalf. We have and will continue to cooperate fully with law enforcement as they conduct their investigation to help with the administration of justice as it should unfold.”

While hazing “might be seen as a tradition creating a sense of belonging and brotherhood,” State Attorney Katherine Fernandez Rundle said those acts amount to crimes with victims in “graves and in hospital beds.”
It wasn’t immediately clear if Pinder, James and Dyous had hired or been assigned attorneys to speak on their behalf.

title: Emily Wilson’s ‘Odyssey’ Translation Inspired the New Movie. Her Review Is Scathing
summary: What “Odyssey” translator and classicist Emily wrote about Christopher Nolan’s movie in her review.
story: Classicist and translator Emily Wilson has some thoughts on Christopher Nolan’s latest blockbuster, “The Odyssey,” calling out the film’s lack of “narrative and emotional depth,” its depiction of the female characters and the misunderstanding of its themes, among many other criticisms.

“The Odyssey,” which hit theaters July 17 and stars Matt Damon, Anne Hathaway, Robert Pattinson, Tom Holland, Zendaya and more famous faces, has received overwhelming praise from fans and critics alike.

The epic, an adaptation of Homer’s ancient Greek poem, has landed at the top of the box office for the last two weeks, already bringing in over $280 million domestically and nearly $640 million worldwide, according to Box Office Mojo. The fantasy flick also debuted with a 98% score on Rotten Tomatoes from critics and has a 97% audience rating as of July 27.
But some classics professors have voiced their issues with the film, most notably Wilson, whose translation of “The Odyssey” influenced Nolan.
Before the film’s release, the auteur quoted Wilson’s translation in a November 2025 interview with Empire.

“I think it’s the Emily Wilson translation that begins, ‘Tell me about a complicated man’,” Nolan said at the time. “The genius of the character, the cleverness, the inventiveness of him, that was a huge part of what interested me. He’s not just a soldier. He’s an amazing strategist, a very wily person.”
After seeing the film, Wilson penned a review for the London Review of Books, which she titled “An Uncomplicated Man.”

In the lengthy critique, Wilson broke down all the areas in which she argues the film fell short, writing that although she was “humbled” when she read Nolan was familiar with her translation, she would have been “ashamed to have written any part of this script.”
Wilson began her review by complimenting Nolan’s version of “The Odyssey” for not being boring.

But she credits that to the strength of the source material. She describes the Oscar-winner’s imagining as “family-friendly audiovisual spectacle, like an elaborate Fourth of July fireworks display — and with about the same level of narrative and emotional depth.”

She noted a pattern of “grandiosity and superficiality” she has seen in some of the director’s past works and similarities particularly in the action-packed sequences. Wilson then mentioned multiple scenes in the movie that she said didn’t elicit an expected emotional reaction, such as the moment Odysseus and his crew sail past the Sirens.
She also said the film is less focused on developing its characters but succeeds “at conveying big bangs and big giants.”
That appears to be the crux of her criticism: the epic tries to do too much.
She wrote, “There is no restraint in Nolan’s version of ‘The Odyssey’: every second is jam-packed with incident, lights and noise, and nothing is ever at a human scale.”
However, one creative choice she didn’t mind was the movie’s the use of American accents and modern contemporary language.

“Despite the manufactured online outrage, there is nothing inherently wrong with the movie’s attempt to approximate contemporary American speech,” she said. “If you’re not going to compose a script in Homeric Greek, or even in metrical English verse, you might as well use something like conversational American English.”
But that doesn’t mean she was a fan of how the choice was executed.
“The language is relentlessly expository, humourless and flat,” Wilson added.
While she applauded some performances, like Hathaway as Penelope and Samantha Moron’s Circe, she said that none of the female characters were portrayed as well as they were written in Homer’s poem.
In summary, “The writing is abysmal. None of the characters has convincing motivation for their actions or words. There are no sex scenes, and all the food looks horrible,” she said.

Although she found the film’s message to be murky, she ended her review explaining why she is still “grateful” the movie was made. She pointed out “The Odyssey”’s worldwide success in a streaming era and how it is driving fans to read multiple translations of the original.

“Nolan, who studied English at University College London — where students still study ‘The Odyssey’ as a first year ‘foundational text’ — is doing his best to get the general public reading again, and I am grateful,” Wilson concludes.
Social media users reacted to her scathing review on X.
Many disagreed with her take, writing that “The Odyssey”’s themes and message about the effects of war were clear.
“I do think The Odyssey had quite a lot to say about war, actually,” one person tweeted.
Another said, “She’s so caught up in literal translations that she’s missing the broader point of a modern interpretation, which stops her from experiencing an excellent film.”
A third agreed that Wilson seemed unwilling to let go of the source material and immerse herself in the adaptation.

“All love to emily wilson who has a way different relationship with the odyssey than the rest of us but that critique is on some level her being unable to reconcile w the fact that this is ‘nolan’s odyssey’, not ‘nolan making homer’s odyssey into a motion picture,” the X user said.
Others shared Wilson’s point of view.
“I love how she defends Nolan’s right to make his own story out it as Homer itself is and then goes to town on what is actually made,” one praised. “This is a great critique piece.”
Another simply said, “Did i love the movie? yes. is emily wilson also correct? Yes.”

title: Keke Palmer Says She Has ‘Genuine Chemistry’ with Sean Evans: ‘Couldn’t Force That If I Tried’
summary: Keke Palmer talks with TODAY with Jenna & Sheinelle about her “chemistry” with “Hot Ones” host Sean Evans.
story: Keke Palmer is setting the record straight on her relationship with “Hot Ones” host and co-creator Sean Evans.

The pair’s chemistry has sparked headlines for years. Evans was a guest on her “Baby, This is Keke Palmer” podcast in May, re-igniting conversation about their connection on social media. A few weeks later, they were spotted having dinner together.
“Our chemistry is genuine ... I couldn’t force that if I tried,” Palmer said July 27 on TODAY with Jenna & Sheinelle. “We always felt that chemistry.”
Things reached a fever pitch when the photo of them having dinner together made the rounds.
“It’s life. Essentially, we met at work. We had chemistry. Work husband, work wife. You just have that chemistry with people,” Palmer said of the dinner. “Then, we hang out.”
Palmer said the response to the photo, and to their perceived connection, has stunned her.
“I was gagged that everybody was ready to marry me off,” she said. “Guys, let it cook! They married your girl off in two seconds!”
In her words, fans “write the story quicker than you can live it.”
Palmer said there’s been no way to avoid the interest from the public.

“I see somebody at the airport. I’m going through TSA. They’re like, ‘So, girl, what’s going on?’” she said. “I’m like, ‘Well, girl, you gotta let time pass. This just happened yesterday.’ So it’s like this thing where, it’s so interesting. It’s so parasocial, the world we live in now.”
The “Nope” actor is not averse to avoiding the dialogue that may exist around her online.

“I do look sometimes, especially because, first of all, I love pop culture, and I like to know what’s going on,” she said. “For me, sometimes the internet can be similar to, that’s like when I’m waking up and I’m watching y’all on the news. It’s like sometimes you need to know, just so you can stay abreast.

“I don’t let it define the way that I think. If anything, I’m always trying to contextualize things. A lot times I feel like people get that about me. You can’t just take everything at face value. You have to be critically thinking about everything you see.”

Talk that Palmer and Evans were romantically involved began in November 2023 after he named Palmer when asked on Amelia Dimoldenberg’s “Chicken Shop Date” if he ever had a crush on a guest. At that point, Palmer had appeared on “Hot Ones” in 2017 and 2021.
Rumors swirled more after Palmer returned to his show in September 2025 and the two kissed.
Last month, Palmer spoke about the relationship while on the panel for Spotify’s Conversations That Channel Culture talk at Cannes Lions.
Podcast host Jay Shetty asked the actor if she was “serious about Sean Evans,” according to People.
“First of all, I love Sean Evans — I love Sean, hey Sean. That’s my guy ... You never know what can arise from there. We just take it day by day. One wing at a time, so to speak,” she added.

title: Carly Simon Reveals She’s Been Diagnosed with Parkinson’s Disease
summary: Carly Simon revealed to NBC News she has been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease and has also been treated for skin cancer.
story: Carly Simon has revealed she has Parkinson’s disease.
The Grammy-winning singer, 83, shared the news July 27 when providing an update on her health and explaining her absence from the public eye.

“So many people have written to me, kindly wondering about my relative silence, asking how I am and what I have been doing. The truth is, I’ve been learning how to live with Parkinson’s disease,” she said in a statement obtained by NBC News.

“It has taken me some time to understand the diagnosis, to adjust to it, and to decide how much I wanted to say about it publicly. Parkinson’s is different for everyone, and it can be unpredictable. Some days I’m so tired I can’t get the day moving at all. On others, it gives me a little more room to move, think, work, and feel like myself.”
Simon said her health challenges began with arthritis in her knees and one of her hips, which prompted joint replacement surgeries but didn’t solve her mobility problems.

“Eventually, there were periods when I could not walk without considerable help,” she said. “My family and I knew that something more was going on. After an extensive evaluation at the Mayo Clinic, I was diagnosed with Parkinson’s.”

The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame member began taking medication to help with her mobility and other symptoms. She also said that while Parkinson’s is thought of as primarily affecting movement, she’s also experienced “anxiety, depression, exhaustion, and apathy.”

“That has been one of the hardest things to explain,” she said. “It is not simply sadness or laziness. It is as though the part of the brain that sends out invitations to participate in life has temporarily misplaced the guest list.”
Simon then said she was treated for basal cell carcinoma on her face that was removed, “but the surgery affected my appearance and made me more self-conscious about being seen in public.”
She said her problems with movement, along with the Parkinson’s, her surgery and the emotional impact of what she was going through, she had decided to retreat from the spotlight.
“But I have not stopped living, and I have not stopped working,” she added, noting she has been recording a new album called “Comes in Waves” and that has provided her some relief.

“Working on the music gave shape to days that did not always have much shape,” she said. “It gave me somewhere to go without having to leave the room. It reminded me that illness can change your life without becoming the whole of your life.

“I do not consider Parkinson’s a gift or a blessing. It is neither. It is difficult, frustrating, and sometimes frightening. I am still learning how to live with it and how to accept it without feeling that I have surrendered something essential.”
Simon thanked all of those people who have helped through her journey.
“These days I move more slowly, I lean on others more than I once did, and I have learned to accept that every day will look a little different. But I am still very much here,” she said.
What Is Parkinson’s Disease?

Parkinson’s disease is a brain disorder that occurs when nerve cells in the area of the brain that controls movement, called the basal ganglia, stop functioning properly or die, according to the National Institute on Aging.

Hallmark symptoms include uncontrolled movements, like shaking and stiffness, as well as struggling with balance or coordination. As the disease progresses, it can harm one’s ability to walk and talk, and result in behavior changes, memory issues, problems sleeping, depression and more.

The disease is most commonly diagnosed in people 60 and over. There is no cure for Parkinson’s, although there are a variety of treatments to lessen symptoms. Doctors typically diagnose the disease by performing a neurological exam and taking a patient’s medical history.
What Type of Cancer Did Carly Simon Have?
The “You’re So Vain” singer shared in her recent health update that she underwent surgery to remove a basal cell carcinoma, a type of skin cancer, from her face.
“Basal cell carcinoma often looks like a slightly transparent bump on the skin, though it can take other forms,”  according to the Mayo Clinic.
It can also look like a brown, black or blue lesion; a scaly patch that grows over time; or a white scar-like lesion.
It most commonly occurs because of exposure to sunlight. Wearing sunscreen and reducing exposure to the sun can decrease the risk of developing basal cell carcinoma.

To prevent skin cancer, the Mayo Clinic recommends staying out of the sun in the middle of the day, applying sunscreen year-round, wearing clothing that covers arms and legs, not using tanning beds, and paying attention to new growths on skin, as well as changes to moles, freckles, bumps and birthmarks.
Simon was also diagnosed with breast cancer in 1997. She underwent surgery and chemotherapy.

Cancer runs in Simon’s family. Her two sisters died of cancer one day apart in 2022. Joanna Simon died of thyroid cancer, one day shy of her 86th birthday. Lucy Simon died of metastatic breast cancer at 82. In 2018, their brother, Peter, the youngest sibling, died of cardiac arrest at age 71, which occurred after he had been diagnosed with cancer.

title: The Internet Reacts to Raising Cane’s AI Chuck Norris Ads: ‘Dystopian’
summary: Social media users might be weirded out by Raising Cane’s AI depiction of Chuck Norris, but his family approves of the National Chicken Finger Day campaign.
story: Raising Cane’s newest spokesperson is not a person at all.

On July 14, the chicken chain announced it is donating $1 from every Box Combo sold on National Chicken Finger Day (July 27) up to $1 million to benefit Kickstart Kids, the martial arts youth development organization co-founded by Chuck Norris.
The actor, who was a close friend of Raising Cane’s founder Todd Graves, died in March at age 86.
For this charity drive, Raising Cane’s has depicted the “Walker Texas Ranger” star in print, video and more by using artificial intelligence — and people online have a lot to say about it.
“why is nobody talking about the fact raising canes is running ai ads,” asked an X user, posting a commercial where an AI Norris uses a disposable straw to dispatch with a henchman.
“Walked in and was dumbfounded by how bad it was,” wrote one Reddit user in a post titled, “Gross Generative AI Chuck Norris Signage.”
“Dystopian,” noted another.
“this actually breaks my heart and i should’ve expected this,” someone else wrote.
“Disgraceful tbh,” posted one more. “billionaire can’t pay an artist a decent wage. Embarrassing.”
A representative for Raising Cane’s tells TODAY.com that these ads were created with the encouragement and approval of the Norris family.
The nationwide campaign spans television, digital, social media, billboards and Raising Cane’s restaurants, and is led by a spot featuring Gena Norris and twins Dakota Norris and Danilee Norris.
In other ads, created with AI and supported by the Norris family, Graves himself teams up with the digitally rendered Chuck to protect their local Raising Cane’s from a siege of masked henchmen.
“Chuck and Todd shared a friendship built on mutual respect, generosity and a belief in helping young people become the best versions of themselves,” Gena Norris said in a press release.

“Chuck would be deeply honored to know that his legacy is continuing in such a meaningful way,” she continues. “Our family is incredibly grateful to Todd and everyone at Raising Cane’s for celebrating my husband’s life and helping carry forward the work that meant so much to him. We’re proud to be part of this campaign and know it will make a difference in the lives of kids across the country.”
In contrast, the family came out against AI-generated videos about the action star’s death in April.

“We are aware that since Chuck’s passing, there have been a number of AI-generated videos and posts circulating online that contain false and misleading information regarding the circumstances of his passing, his health history, and who was present,” read a statement posted to his Instagram stories, according to Variety.
